This might be the game that actually attracts a younger newer audience like the original game did back in 1994.

Currently it is only single player with 4 or 5 single player missions done, and a huge selection of survival maps with interesting waves of enemies, bosses, upgrades, and a variety of online difficulty score boards for each map. Even with this, you get a feel for the guns, the AI, the flying machanics, and some level layouts that show off their new cube system for maps. I'd say, wait for release if you can (because thats when the multiplayer should start rolling out), or get it now and enjoy some nice score board competition with friends.

I'm only 2 hours in and already I'm hooked. Overload is a blast and represents a piece of gaming that's been lost to us for so long and I am HERE for it. This is what I've been waiting for decades to have again and if it wasn't for the imminent release of From software's return to the Armoured Core series later this month I would be spending every gaming second playing the bejeezus out of this little gem.

For the uninitiated, Overload is a "6 degrees of freedom" (6DOF) shooter. If you like FPS games, imagine doom, but where you are essentially floating all the time and can go up and down at will as well as left, right forward back and the usual strafing movements. While it sounds like it can be confusing, it quickly becomes intuitive to move around as the controls are basically standard FPS controls with the ability to 'fly' wherever you want by pushing forward to move wherever your camera is pointing, even if that's straight up. This lends a measure of verticality to the level designs that makes your environments more immersive and combats more strategic and more intense than your average FPS. 

Overload lays on the atmosphere thick, borrowing every cue it can from it's spiritual predecessor, Descent. The sound cues, colour palette, level atmosphere, gameplay loop and even the 'corporate doing bad things' story  are taken almost wholesale from Descent so you'll feel right at home if you've come from the any of the Descent series. If what you were looking for in a game was "Descent, but modern" and somehow you missed this, stop reading my review and but this right now - you will not be disappointed at all.   If you don't know what descent is, read on and I'll tell you why this may appeal to you.

Imagine flying through a starbase or the innards of a moon in a space hovercraft armed to the teeth where every robot worker you meet wants you dead. As you work your way through the environment uncovering tunnels, rescuing colonists in cryosleep, you're looking for a reactor to detonate the facility and wipe out all the robots and whatever naughty things the bad corporate types were up to in one fell swoop. You set off the reactor's meltdown sequence and then realise, " I can't teleport out!" so now you have to dash back through the facility looking for an emergency exit before you explode with the facility....
It's a rush and a far more atmospheric and tactical experience than 90% of traditional FPS games. If the passage above piques your interest or makes you think "That could be fun" then Overload is for you. Go get it. 

If you are still on the fence, 6DOF style games bridge a gap between space combat sims like colony wars, X-wing/Squadrons or Wing Commander and traditional FPS games like Doom, Rise of the Triad, Duke Nukem, or Serious Sam. I draw the Doom comparison more due to the themes (moonbases where bad stuff happens and what was once good now becomes bad). People who like the idea of Space Combat but who typical can't get along with target tracking or flight controls will find 6DOF style games better suited to them as a 6DOF game doesn't have the typical flight control issues, target tracking or constant moving. If you stop, you hover. So, if you are worried about tracking targets or getting lost, don't worry. this game feels like playing Doom but where you have wings. 

While Overload seems to have been written for people missing Descent (like me!), the devs have made this a very friendly experience for people new to the genre. Multiple difficulty modes, an excellent automap, a little drone to help you find your way around if you get lost, a clean UI, accessibility tools, fully remappable controls and controller support with a well thought out default control scheme help a newbie get involved at their pace easily. There's also a great training mode and plenty of things to find that isn't just "shoot the bad guy and panic" so the gameplay loop doesn't feel stale as you learn. Getting started is easy and if you are used to FPS games rather than flight sim games you can even invert your Y axis to act more like you'd be used to in a traditional FPS game. 

For the vets of 6DOF games all the options you'd expect are here: Multiple weapons to discover, upgrade paths for your arsenal, plenty of secrets to find, story bites through discoverable audio logs, mouse and keyboard or flight yoke support, a plethora of graphics and audio options, VR support, online multiplayer. There's a lot to like here for the newcomer or the veteran.  

In play, the game is smooth and the textures work well. Lighting is nice and the flares/headlamps work very well to light darker spaces. Control is smooth, whatever methods you choose, and audio cues for waiting robot foes are present so you can be clued in on imminent ambushes or hidden doorways. The map is so much better than the old Descent map and reminds me a lot of Sublevel Zero's map system. Audio in combat is meaty and the weapons feel varied with some thought put in to how to make the various missiles look and feel different from one another both is visuals and effect.

As far as drawbacks are concerned there is one I've encountered - interactables in the environment aren't always super clear. The first you come across is a big red button. When you see it for the first time you may dismiss it as a light or a grill but once you know what it is you'll be looking for more. It's, admittedly, a minor gripe in an otherwise excellent game.

If you are looking for a 6DOF or your next Descent-style fix, or if you want something different from your usual FPS or space combat games, Overload has what you want. Get it, get lost in it's winding tunnels, let the story carry you away and try not to call yourself Material Defender while you're scrapping robots.

This review is from my experience in SP.  Haven't played MP yet, but MP is just a bonus for me.  

We've waited forever for a new Descent game.  There have been some solid 6DOF games in the past 15+ years, but none of them get the feel right.  However, this isn't some cheap knock-off made by a different company.  This game is made by the guys who created it to begin with and understand how a Descent game should play and feel.  Everything about this is smooth.  It controls beautifully, and blowing up robots has the right amount of punch to make it satisfying.  The weapons are fun to shoot and varied enough to allow for different play styles.  The levels are well designed and interesting enough to make me want to explore to find all the powerups and secrets.  The story is interesting enough that I actually don't mind that they don't have the rights to the story and setting from Descent, and I actually like the audio clips that you collect in the levels a lot.  There is also a pretty fun horde mode which provides some single player replayability (though the campaign is worth playing again at harder difficulties and to find all the secrets). 

It's hard for me to complain about anything in this game as its pretty much exactly what I wanted - basically Descent 1+2 updated for the modern age.  It's simple, but it should be.  I've heard that the Multiplayer matchmaking system could use some work, so there is that.

If you like Descent buy this game and support these guys.  They did a great job and I think there is more to come.

I begged my parents to buy the game, went home and installed it on my powerhouse Pentium 2 450 Mhz PC. I was in gaming heaven. Fast forward 28 years and somehow I stumble across this gem in Steam. Forget the rest, this is the Descent successor you need to get.  Descent I and Descent II were easily my most played games of all time.  Hundreds and hundreds of teenage hours poured in to those 6 degrees of freedom.  I wouldn't hesitate for a second to say the Descent series were my all-time favorite games.  Even in recent years I would dig out my old CDs and boot up a engine replacement and blast some bots.  The Descent II soundtrack has a permanent place on my iPhone MP3 list and I listen to it all the time.  Back in the day I used to spend HOURS in Polyedit and HAMM and Yahoma and Descent Manager trying to make my own mission pack.  I was on the Descent Editors mail list, and even contributed voice work to a fan-made mission pack that was on the Silent Threat add-on for Descent: Freespace.  That's how much of a Descent fan I am.

Other Descent-alikes have come and go, some were fun, some were okayish.  The new Descent that was Kickstarted a couple years ago was a good attempt but still doesn't feel "right" to me.

This.  This game feels RIGHT.  The bots, the maps, the weapons, the sounds, the music, the fluidity of the controls.  It's all Descent.  This game could be Descent IV and you'd never even question it for a second, heck, it'd probably be considered better than Descent III.  The first map just blew me away.  It was like I was teleported back to 1995 being 13 and playing Descent I for the first time.

[b][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/448850/]Overload[/url][/b] is an awesome modern replacement for the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/bundle/5605/]The Descent Classic Collection[/url]!  I didn't even know this game existed until I saw it was part of the June 2020 [url=https://www.humblebundle.com/subscription]Humble Bundle Choice[/url].  This is what the now-dead [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/360950/]Descent: Underground[/url] could have been.  

The first thing that struck me was the perspective-curved menu, which was fresh and modern.  I enjoyed working my way through the levels, trying to find the security keys, finding secrets and secret levels, destroying enemies in spectacular explosions, and trying to stay alive to accomplish the missions.  There's a ship upgrade system to help your ship to overcome stronger enemies, or more difficult levels, requiring you to discover upgrade tokens hidden through the levels in order to take advantage of.  The game itself looks and plays great, being quite sharp and highly polished.  It has trading cards, lots of achievements, a free [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/884970/]Overload Level Editor[/url], built-in cross-platform multiplayer modes, and also mod support.

It's easy to become disoriented while playing, due to the [i]six-degree-of-freedom (6DoF)[/i] nature of the game, just like the original [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/273570/]Descent[/url]. To offset this, you're provided with a 3D level-map to help you find your way if you're lost, which can also be used to help you find secrets.  In addition to this, you have flares and headlights built into your ship to help you navigate darker sections of a level, and a holographic guide-bot to lead you to where you want to go.

On the downside, the Internet multiplayer aspect of it could have been improved, because you need to find the IP address of a server to join using a web browser, and I felt an in-game server listing would have helped immensely.

Aside from that, I highly recommend this game if you're even slightly a fan of any games in [url=https://store.steampowered.com/bundle/5605/]The Descent Classic Collection[/url], because [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/448850/]Overload[/url] is clearly the spiritual successor of them all!  If you are interested in the genre, or want to give 6DoF a try, you don't want to miss this game!

Overload is a retread, in this case of Descent and Descent 2 (1994 and 1996, respectively). And it turns out that’s 100% okay, because Descent was the path not followed; in the 19 years since Descent 3 was released, almost no games have tackled the “six degrees of freedom” shooter, with mainstream shooters having moved in the opposite direction. The few that did were either underbaked or something substantially different (namely, the roguelike shenanigans of Sublevel Zero).

Overload is fast & frenetic, combining subterranean maze navigation, twitching shooting, fancy piloting, and secret hunting into an adrenaline-filled package that’s smooth as butter. The levels are big enough to allow for real exploration but small enough to prevent you from being totally lost, and new enemies and weapons are introduced at a rapid clip. There’s a handy, retro 3D automap, and the “guidebot” from Descent 2 returns to provide a more naturalistic way to hunt down enemies, power-ups and objectives than the giant floating HUD markers favored by modern open-world games.

It’s not entirely without its faults–RPS forumite Godwhacker summarized them well when he noted that “a) there’s only one enemy AI behaviour, which is the classic ‘float forwards shooting’ and b) they’d put secrets in every level but implemented them Wolfenstein 3D style, with the only way of finding them being shooting every wall.” But neither of these significantly reduced the fun I had digging out my HOTAS and blowing up robots while spinning in circles likely to make onlookers nauseous.

If you don't know what "Descent" is, that's a game where you played on a spaceship from the perspective of the cockpit and you'd move through some pretty narrow and constrained pathways within labyrinthine levels as you fought different enemies.

This is much of that, but it has some cool modern features, such as better graphics, a robot that you can call to guide you through your objective with the "Z" key -by default-, and finally, it has a lot of difficulty settings. So you get some that are quite easy, and some that are quite difficult like the original "Descent" was. The normal difficulty ("Rookie" mode) starts off fairly easy and quickly turns into a very tough experience after a while, but it never feels unfair and the game uses a manual saving system. So you can quicksave your way through the game.

The game also included upgrades for your weapons and ship, so you can increase the speed, damage, and even get different weapons as you play along. It can be a bit overwhelming to play the game from the perspective of the cockpit though, a lot of the times you can get swarmed and not even understand what's happening on the screen anymore. But it's still good fun.

Recommend it.

This brings back the feeling I had playing Descent 1 + 2 back in the days. It's a good example of how it is possible to polish established gameplay without all this modern "open world", "procedural generation", "pay to win"-stuff which all games seem to include these days. Combat is smooth, fast-paced and at times daunting. In the old Descent I used to be able to retreat to other parts of the level to restock, here you need to actually get into the thick of it, especially if there are fabricators around.

The upgrade and experience system gives players an incentive to give replay the single player campaign and discover all the secrets. It's a cleverly featured role-playing element.

The graphics are superb, however the colour palette seems to have little variation and also the operators look rather similar.  I could identify the robots easier in the old Descent games. Here, you need to wait for shots fired, to realize what you're up against. Also the explosions, while rather impressive, seem to clutter everything up.

Sound and music however seem very punchy, something I liked in the prequels as well. There is plenty of bass to listen to, when you fire your weapons and blow things up.

Enough reviewing, I'm going back to more gaming. Looks like this will keep me satisfied for a long time :)

Remember the sci-fi simulator Descent? Overload is the same!

Descent is one of those games that players in their thirties remember with a nostalgic tear in their eyes. While the younger ones probably have no idea what Descent is. Now all generations of players can experience what flying in narrow tunnels is like. Or in closed rooms, where swarms of robotic enemies are pouring in on you from all sides.

Overload is basically the same as the original DESCENT. Anyone who has ever played Descent will immediately know that these two games have the same genetic basis.

Your opponents fall into four categories. The most numerous group are those who are trying to pierce you with beam weapons. Then there are those who shoot you with rockets from a distance, at best with unguided ones. The third group is represented by robotic drones who want to share it with you up close. And the last category is kamikaze robots that rush to you and detonate. Enemies often understandably attack in mixed groups.

You can gradually hang up to sixteen different weapons on your battleship. There are either cannons (energy or projectile) or a wide range of missiles:

In addition to the story campaign, Overload also offers multiplayer competitions and an endless mode where you can test your reflexes and accuracy. That is, provided that all those turns, turns and quick movements do not make you sick.

     Graphically, the game looks decent, the sound and music are ok. Overload is well optimized and does not require disk space. I would recommend it especially to those who still remember Descent and want to relive the challenge of a tunnel shooter.

     And I secretly hope to see a remake of Descent: Freespace, which in its time offered experiences comparable to the Star Wars space battles. Even without claustrophobic levels, with giant enemy cruisers.

In short: 

This game is literally Descent. You may make your own mind up as to whether or not that's a recommendation.

To go into more detail:

Were you born in the late 80s or early 90s? Did play flight-sim/shoot-'em-up hybrids like Hellbender and Descent religiously? Do you enjoy the thought of guiltlessly murdering a variety of hovering robots with a colourful selection of guns and missiles? Do you like flying around in extremely constrained spaces?

Congratulations - you will love this game!

When I write reviews on Steam, I try to shy away from the whole "if you liked X, then you'll love this game" cliché, but in this case I think it's appropriate. If you liked Descent or any of its direct sequels, you will very likely love this game, because it's literally just Descent but with better graphics. All the guns and missiles are more or less straight ports of weapons from the old games with new names. The robots are different to some degree, but even there I could see some obvious design similarities. Everything is more or less the same.

This also includes the claustrophobic, labyrinthine level design, the dozens of genuinely secret secret areas in each level, the fast-paced, nerve-racking gameplay and a pretty period-accurate soundtrack. The controls need a little bit of work here and there, but they're generally as tight and responsive as I remember then being back when I was 9 and only very slightly worse at video games than I am at 29.

Beyond a fairly simple upgrade system, this game makes no real attempt to innovate on the Descent formula. The slight changes it makes to core systems from the old games feel like additions that should always have been there. And for fans of Descent 3, I should say that aside from the general look and feel of the game, this game cribs far more heavily from Descent 1 and Descent 2 than the third installment. You shouldn't expect any wide-open outdoor spaces, mission control updates or gigantic set-piece boss fights in this game.

I had genuine fun playing the four missions currently available for this game, and it's one of the few Early Access titles I felt was genuinely worth my money. I can't say for sure whether you'll feel the same. This game is decidedly a nostalgia trip, and if you were never a fan of Descent or you want something that takes the genre some place new, this game will not satisfy you.

But I loved it.

Descent 2.5, Descent 2 brought to modern standards, Descent 2-2, whatever ya wanna call it. The OG Descent devs got together to make a spiritual successor to a classic, but forgotten FPS series, And boy what a ride it is!

For those of you who are unfamiliar a bit of a history lesson. Descent was released in 1995 by Parralax Software, it was a First person shooter that used an honest-to-goodness 3D engine and instead of being locked on the floor and running around as an infantryman, like in every other FPS game before and most since, you are in a Zero-G environment and pilot a vehicle thats more akin to an Attack helicopter with an array of energy weapons and missiles, only you can freely rotate, and strafe in any Axis. You thought circle strafing in quake or unreal was nuts, Add a vertical element to it! And there you have Descent! You fought Mining and security robots gone hayware from a computer virus in all the games, rarely killing actual people (Mostly accidentally in 3, completley on purpose in 3 Mercs). I completely missed out on underground but I've heard it ended up being and unfinished buggy multiplayer-focused mess that was canned by a shady publisher who screwed the developers over in the end.

As A kid I played a LOT of Descent 1 and 3, never quite beating them (1 had limited lives and very long levels, 3 was buggy and I could not progress due to a crash bug on the moon mission, I did play and beat the uneven Mercenaries expansion however), only picking up 2 when it became available for GOG, 2 Ended up being my favorite of the three for its incredible pacing, UX improvements, and Soundtrack (nevermind some VERY satisfying weaponry). 

1 was innovative and a technical marvel at the time but could be a slog and had cheap enemies. 2 Ironed out a lot of 1's rough edges, by introducing an optional guide bot that was locked behind a cage at the start of each mission that would lead you to each key and eventually to the reactor or boss, passing up secrets as a drawback (it would come back annoy you like Navi or Fi in the Legend of Zelda games if you deviated from the path). and 3 (and it's expansion Mercenaries) was structured a little more like Goldeneye over DOOM, being more objective focused rather than "Get all the keys and kill the reactior and escape" adding in puzzle elements to the mix, while it helped vary up the level design, the implementation was hit-or-miss.

The reason why I went on this history lesson is because Overload Faithfully preserves everything good about D 1-2 (and some elements of 3, like being able to spawn your guidebot anywhere and some weapons) and then improves on nearly everything it brings back. Really writing the history of the descent games will explain 80% of what overload is

Descent's weapons did feel kind of samey but in Overload, They all have different tactical applications and gimmicks. There's even an upgrade system that allows you to fine tune your playstyle and encourages exploration more! Audio logs flesh out the story, SPAWNERS CAN FINALLY BE DESTROYED, and modern options can even help alleviate some of the motion sickness the series is famous for inducing (FOV Sliders reportedly, I never had this issue but I know its been a hard sell when I try and hype it up to my friends)

And if you want it Has VR!

This is a Descent clone, made by a lot of the people behind the original Descent series. If you haven't played the original Descent series it was both the first FPS with true 3d graphics and the first shooter in a zero gravity environment. Descent has very sprawling maze-like levels with plenty of Doom-like secret doorways and hidden goodies and that's all present in Overload as well.

+ Controls have been modernised, it's easy to drop in and play I didn't rebind any keys, didn't even feel the need to change mouse sensitivity. Your ship has weight to it and is very easy to control.
+ Lockdown sections (especially the optional ones) explore how different enemies act and work together and put you in an isolated arena suited to those enemies strengths. These sections really stood out in the overall level design.
+ Hidden goodies are easier to find, thanks to better graphical fidelity you can see the seams where wall panels might slide away to reveal a hidden room or cubby.
+ Enemy AI employs a range of tactics. Some enemies are just dumb and sit in place shooting at you. Some will fire off a salvo and run away behind a corner to surprise you later, others will aim to ram into you and if they miss will continue to attack you from behind, others will actively set up flanks and others still will attack head on in a pack and dart away to pull your attention in 3 different directions.
+ Thanks to enemy AI being at the level it is, it's very satisfying to trash them. It actually does sometimes feel like you're outsmarting them.
+ On that note, horde mode! Trash as many bots as you can without dying and make it on to the leaderboards.
+ Weapons are all made to fill a niche and can be upgraded and specialised.
+ No hit-scan weapons, weighty turn speed. You can avoid most shots and you can exploit some enemies slow turning speed to get yourself into their blindspots if you're quick enough.
+ Multiple difficulty settings to offer a nice consistent challenge.

+/- Maze like map design

- Grey rock tunnels look the same in both directions. Overload takes a realistic approach to decorating levels as opposed to Descent with its purple cave walls and running water (on an asteroid) on the floor (in zero-G). Everything looks a lot better but reorienting yourself without those hints is more of a challenge. It's a tradeoff, luckily the minimap is very good.
- There are two pairs of "model twins" among enemies, Goblins and Ogres share the same profile as do Gorgons and Krakens. It's not a mistake you'll make after a couple of hours in game but it's an exceedingly painful mistake for those couple of hours because in both cases one twin is mostly harmless and the other will happily burst you down at medium range. I can't help but compare to Descent once again, not only did each enemy design have its own unique garish paint job but they were also all radically different shapes so none of their targeting profiles blurred together. This is again a tradeoff with graphical fidelity, thanks to all the pretty lighting and reflections it's hard to tell what kind of paintjob a particular bot has at a glance.

Not just some soulless Descent nostalgia cashgrab, Overload is a very worthy sequel to the series. 
There are so many thoughtful design improvements over the original games that fans of Descent will welcome, such as the ability to destroy enemy spawners, and much thought given to the balance of the new weapon set. You'll quickly find ideal situations for weapons, and the upgrades will satisfy all your immediate thoughts of "This weapon would be so much more useful if..."

Newcomers who haven't played Descent may find the controls awkward at first, due to the uncommon nature of moving in all 3 dimensions and the fact that you are steering a ship rather than aiming a gun, but the game feels just as at home with a mouse as it does with a joystick, due to increased max turn speeds compared to Descent (yet the ability to limit it to feel more like it). So, the barrier for adjustment is not high.

Levels feel most like Descent 2, with more open rooms and not just cramped tunnels. Cool VR support is a nice bonus to the game, looking around the cockpit looks like a blast, though I do not have a VR headset myself to know...

The only real complaints I have are that the enemy AI feels much more simplistic compared to Descent, enemies tend to only move towards you and shoot, only sometimes dodging or retreating. Despite being a pretty big fan of Freespace, I've never tried any of the Descent games—Descent is basically only connected to Freespace 1 by a colon in the title, so they just never really crossed my radar. I probably should've played them a long time ago, though, because their spiritual successor Overload is pretty damn awesome.

Developed by many former Descent devs and poaching most of the main gameplay mechanics, Overload is a generally fantastic game. Working as a kind of 360 degree Doom, you traverse claustrophobic bases in a very agile ship, strafing and flipping in any direction as needed to navigate. It's a huge shift from what I've come to expect in the more traditional space sim, which was a pleasant surprise! Overload combines all the freedom of movement I love in space dogfights with the twitchy paranoia of corridors filled with things that want to kill you. 

It all culminates in a thrilling rush to the exit after blowing a generator, twisting, boosting and manoeuvring quick as you can through the squadrons spawned to get in the way. It's a gimmick lifted completely from Descent, but I can see why because it's easily the best part of any level, desperately trying to stay oriented and keep your bearings while your screen visually assaults you will explosions. 

Even the story is a lot better than the average 90s shooter. When I first picked up Overload I played usually one or two levels a day before moving on to whatever bigger game I was working on. But by the midpoint or so, I was getting pretty interested in what would come next, both in terms of plot and level design. By the end, I beat the last five levels in one sitting—thoroughly hooked, if you couldn't tell.

Being unfamiliar with Overload's main inspiration I'm sure I missed a bunch of other shout-outs and design refinements, but the point is that Overload is super fun even without the nostalgia—the best of both worlds that every Kickstarter retro revival should try to hit. It's a criminally underrated game—likely done in by the cult space sim audience and impossible to Google name—and well worth picking up as a sleek, modern entry point to the spaceflight genre.

One of the very first PC games I played, before even owning a PC, was Descent.  I had no idea how to play, I was a little kid doing everything wrong.  I thought shooting flares was my gun.  I achieved nothing except wonderment at the idea of a 3D game where you fly around and fight robots.  Now 20-some years later I got to try my hand at the spiritual successor, Overload, and this time… I know how to shoot. 

[h1] A Brief History [/h1]

Overload was kickstarter funded in March of 2016 and went into development under Revival Productions, a team with members of the original Descent team.  It was released just over two years later in May of 2018.  The whole event snuck under my radar.  Probably because I had my gaze focused on another Descent spiritual successor, Descent: Underground.  A game also successfully crowdfunded with some former Star Citizen developers.  However, unlike Overload, it had a much more rocky release and is currently back in development for a single player campaign.

[h1] On to the Actual Game [/h1]

I have to start by saying this game is definitively representative of Descent as my nostalgia-riddled mind can remember it.  It really feels as close to the original game in all of the core aspects.  I know most people aren’t familiar with games well over two decades old, but luckily you can still buy and play all of the original series on Steam.  Nice, right?  Yet, if you don’t want to jump back in time, Overload brings back a much of the gameplay, but with a wonderful rendition of modern graphics.    

What sets Overload apart from the modern resurgence of space dogfighting games is how it squeezes you in to tight spaces and down narrow maze-like hallways.  I’m not using “maze-like” loosely here, with the nature of your ability to fly in any direction and roll 360 degrees without much defining what is up or down, it’s incredibly easy to get lost in this game.  Navigation, of course, is used as one of the main components in the challenge of the gameplay.  The level design has you traveling into random corners and through hidden doorways to both find secret bonus items and upgrades as well as progress through the game itself.  It can easily be overwhelming, especially early on, as you desperately dip in and out of the massive 3D rendered map looking for some hallway or doorway you missed.  To combat this, Overload includes a ‘hologuide’ that you can pop up at any time that will lead you to the next objective, whether that’s the end of the level or just another key to unlock a door.   

[h1] Fight the Power [/h1]

As you progress through the relatively short story and it’s 15 levels, your biggest hurdle outside of figuring out where the hell to go is shooting your many different weapons at a decently diverse set of enemies.  You end up with eight standard weapons that pull from two pools, energy and ammo , as well as eight secondary weapons in the form of various missiles, rockets, and mines that have a wider variety of functionality, but a much smaller pool of ammo.  While on the relatively low difficulty that I played, ammo was more than abundant, it is important to make sure you use weapons efficiently and swap regularly for what best fits the situation.  You can (and should) spend time exploring levels to find upgrade points that you can use to make weapons do more damage, fire faster, or in some way increase their effectiveness.  In addition to this, you have to split the limited points with upgrading other portions of your ship like its health and speed, which can be just as important when things are getting out of hand.  

It may not seem like it at first, but things will get chaotic as enemies can be generated from spawners (that you can destroy) and some are particularly good making things hectic by charging right at your face for massive damage or filing the screen with explosives.   Overload’s level design is specifically tailored to allow these enemy robots appear out of hidden doors and from around corners to be extra effective with their attacks.  The oddly Jurassic way they often roar when they attack from that hiding spot makes for tense moments as well.  Yet it doesn’t really step into the realm of the tension you’d feel in a survival horror game since you’re armed to the teeth with robot shredding weaponry.

[h1] Cherry Picking the Past [/h1]

Overload gets a lot of things right.  It has plenty of action, tons of secrets and exploration for the people who are willing to dive into that insanity, and even a decent story that gets moving as the game progresses.  The soundtrack is a little hit or miss, but is very prominent throughout, so that could be a strong point for some as well.  If you look at the campaign alone it is a bit short, but if you’re a completionist, you enjoy challenge levels, or you manage to find some people online to play the multiplayer with, you can sink many more hours into the game.  It could probably also benefit from a little more visual design variety since nearly every level features the same gray walls and industrial assets with rock caves thrown in randomly.  It also wouldn’t hurt to see a little more variety in the objective types for each level, where the vast majority are simply destroying a reactor.  Yet, even with those issues it’s not hard to see that this is a great spiritual successor and fun to play.  However, at this point seven months after release, it’s probably safe to say you should be looking for it a good bit less than the base $30 price tag.

I think we have the privilege these days of a nice combination of accessible game development tools and a huge history of great games that can be revisited to entertain old fans and make new ones.  Overload took a classic franchise of the past and built a game that not only appeals to the old farts that enjoyed it back then, but can also be appreciated by people who weren’t even alive when Descent was in stores (on shelves, you had to go pick up a giant box, it was cool).  That quality is sometimes forgotten in modern remakes and spiritual successors, and I’m always happy to see a one that has a potential for broad spectrum appeal.

While it may not officially carry the Descent name, Overload was developed by many of the same people behind the original Descent franchise, and it shows!  It feels exactly like a new and modernized addition to the Descent series and I couldn't be happier with it - especially since the official Descent Underground title is beleaguered by legal troubles and may never even see the light of day.  I commend the Revival Productions team, who raised half as much money as Descendent Studios to develop their new game, and delivered this rock solid title just over two years later.  By comparison, two years after Descendent Studios' Kickstarter we instead saw Descent Underground removed from Steam Early Access, and nearly three years after that we are still left waiting for any meaningful progress.

+ Modern features
VR support, Tobii eye tracking support, and surround sound audio really take the immersion to the next level - provided you can afford all those accessories and peripherals.

+ Great controls
I love games that let me take full advantage of my Steam controller, and gyro controls really shine with this title.  6DOF games do come with a somewhat steep learning curve, it can take some time to get the hang of navigating and aiming accurately, but using a Steam controller made this less difficult.  You can easily map any other gamepad or joystick you have instead if you prefer.  It is definitely more challenging to play with just a keyboard and mouse however.

+ That Descent feel
The story, the level design and lighting, the models of the enemy robots, the weapons, the sound effects, the music - all of it will bring back that Descent nostalgia by being just similar enough to the original series.  As a fan who played countless hours of the original trilogy of Descent games, I loved every moment of this game.

Other thoughts...

* This game is hard.
I've seen a number of reviews complaining about the difficulty of this game, from the hoards of robots you face during later levels to how hard it can be to locate all of the secrets within the maps.  These are not negatives but positives in my opinion.  I'm honestly tired of how most modern games hold your hand too much and don't present you with a real challenge.  There will be none of that here with Overload.

* Multiplayer, but not enough players
There's maybe at best 30 players online at one time, so while the game supports multiplayer, unless you bring your own friends to play with you there sadly isn't in reality much multiplayer action to be had.  Unfortunately 6DOF games don't have a very big player base to begin with.

* Built on Unity?!
Usually I can tell right away that I am playing a game built on Unity by the obvious lack of quality.  It is very easy for a developer to build a mediocre game on Unity, it is much harder to build a good game on Unity that doesn't immediately look and feel like a Unity game.  Further testament to the skills of the Revival Productions dev team for managing to make such a quality title on this second rate game engine.

This game is to Descent what Doom (2016) was for.. erm.. Doom (1994).  It resurrects the spirit of the franchise while eliminating the less favorable aspects from the original.  It also adds new gameplay features, very similar to the same way that Doom (2016) did.  Upgrade points are available to spend that improve your ship and weapons from mission-to-mission.  There are legions of secrets and time-challenges to discover.  The soundtrack is superb.  Levels are mazes to race through, blasting enemies with an ever-expanding arsenal of destructive weaponry.  I was a huge Descent 3 fan back in the day and it is so gratifying to see this sub-genre come back with such polish.

----------------------------------------------------
If you've played Descent
----------------------------------------------------
It's literally Descent 4 under a different name, so if you enjoyed the previous games, get this one. New maps, new weapons, new enemies, epic new soundtrack. The graphics aren't as revolutionary as Descent and Descent 3 were for their time, but it gets the job done.

The biggest criticism I can level against it from the perspective a Descent veteran is that it doesn't evolve the formula a lot. It's a pretty "safe" game from the perspective of, it didn't try anything really outside the box from previous games in the series: It's still a linear string of missions with a few secret levels on the side, it's still you against world, it's it's still a matter of finding and blowing the reactor then finding the escape tunnel.  It would have been nice to see them try something like adding allies, strategic/resource-management gameplay, an overworld, dynamic loot, etc etc. The most significant addition is the upgrade points system which.... It's not *bad*, but they don't let you reassign points or really specialize into any one area. There's only 2 upgrade levels per system and if you explore levels thoroughly you'll get a ton of upgrades, so there's really no concept of replaying the campaign over with different a different loadout e.g. specifically a cannon sniper, or a missile boat, or a minelayer.


----------------------------------------------------
If you have not played Descent
----------------------------------------------------
This is a "6 degrees of freedom" game (6DOF), where you pilot a space ship through zero-gravity environments. You can yaw, pitch and roll like an aircraft, move backward and forward, and also slide laterally up/down or left/right.  Getting used to the controls might take a little but, the smooth flight physics and total freedom makes just getting around the levels feel enjoyable in itself.

You'll pick up a variety of primary weapons (machine guns and laser type things) and secondary weapons (rockets, missiles and bombs) and be able to use both of these simultaneously. Secondary weapons tend to pack a big punch but ammunition is fairly limited, while your primaries use energy or bullets which are plentiful. Each weapon is aimed at specific tactical scenario, and learning to quickly recognize the best weapon for a given situation and deploy it is key.

Levels are large and complicated. The 6DOF flight model means that you will be twisting and turning in every direction. Levels usually have a general sense of "this way up",  but doors and hallways will often split off at all kinds of crazy directions. There is an auto map feature in the game to help you find your way around by showing you where you  have been and where you have not, and there's also a friendly guide bot that can lead you. So navigating the levels requires some lateral thinking but are not intended to literally be mazes.

Enemies? There's lots of enemies to shoot at. The story is the classic AI-gone-rogue horror show, where all of the machines meant to build, mine, and defend the space colonies have gone haywire and now attack you on sight. There's a good variety of different robots, which though they kind of look similar, have very different weapons and tactics. Some robots are relatively stupid and just lumber in your general direction firing off plasma cannons, while other robots are weak and sneaky and like to shoot missiles at you while your back is turned then run away.  There's even melee robots that will rush at you and try to dismantle your ship with buzz saws and giant claws. Robots are generally smart, challenging, and you'd swear they are actually working together sometimes....

Descent has always been something of the odd man out in the pantheon of FPS classics. Despite innovating on the basic first-person formula with its six-degrees-of-freedom free-flight combat, it never took off or spawned the slew of imitators its peers did. It did get two sequels and a brilliant spin-off space sim series, though, and now after far too long it has returned. Only now it’s called Overload, and all the names are different. The head-spinning combat and ravenous robots and flashy weapons and explosive escapes are all back, along with a few new tricks learned in the intervening decade. But in some ways, Overload might be a little too tethered to its ancestors to really rise to its occasion.

Space mining corp Juno Offworld has pushed out to the moons of Saturn with their Cronus Frontier initiative, a network of bases manned by skeleton crews and worked by robotic autonomous operators. Something has gone drastically wrong though, and the auto-ops have begun taking their mining lasers and rock crushers to the humans instead of the minerals. Your ship, the Iberia, just happens to be in the right place to intervene and happens to have a smart little gunship for you to pilot on search and destroy missions. To root out whatever madness is afoot you’ll need to battle back the auto-ops and destroy the reactors of the fallen facilities, hopefully escaping the blast in the process.

The formula is very much the same as in the first two Descents, but new to Overload is a fairly involved story. The pre-mission briefings drop tons of tidbits about what’s going on in Saturn’s orbit as you gear for your next assault, and each mission has a bunch of concise audio logs that detail the strange machinations that led to the robot rebellion. Eventually the many plot threads weave together to explain the whole mess and point you to a final showdown that… honestly only resolves a small piece of the story. I’ll forgive them a weak ending for keeping the narrative running just through text and logs, because there’s a surprising amount going on that you only really hear about.

Your concern is going to be getting in, blowing everything up, and getting back in one piece, and that won’t be a simple task. Being a six-degrees-of-freedom game, you have the ability to fully traverse the cavernous chambers and winding passages of each facility. These places are packed with deadly robots, with smarter and fiercer ones appearing the further into the adventure you get. Battles are hectic, with you dodging lasers and missiles from every angle and returning fire with your own impressive arsenal. As you progress you’ll unlock gatling lasers, flak cannons, homing missiles, room-clearing warheads, and even exotic tools like time-dilating bombs and vortex-generating missiles.

Finding secrets earns you upgrade points to improve your arms, and this part of the game deserves special note. Overload is absolutely THICK with secrets, tucking away literally dozens per mission. They can be as simple as a floor panel that slides open when you bump it, or a button hidden behind a grating that drops the forcefield around a reactor that powers another forcefield that leads to a maze of tunnels loaded with enemies and items. The upgrade points you find are split into two types, normal and super, used to upgrade each weapon twice. The normal upgrade usually gives a single bonus like more damage or a new feature like enemy tracking, while the super upgrade lets you pick one of two powerful suites of improvements. Even if you’re not dogged in your search for secrets you’ll be able to upgrade your favorite weapons, but if you’re the obsessive type you’ll come out with a devastating arsenal.

And you kinda need it, because Overload can get pretty brutal. I say this fully acknowledging there are five difficulty levels and you can switch at any time, but I was determined to beat the third and while I did, it wasn’t always a pleasant experience. The early levels ease you into fighting dangerous auto-ops and big swarms, and the middle levels ramp this up to a thrilling challenge. By mission 11 it was getting a little ridiculous, as new enemies could pound my armor down to nothing in an instant if I ever failed to dodge or juke a salvo. There are no checkpoints either, so I resorted to saving regularly once missions got to be 40 minutes long and the risk of failing an escape at the very end became real. It’s also worth mentioning that the last four missions of the game have a significant change of pace that I found more frustrating than anything.

Overload fits right in with the recent wave of aggressively-retro FPSes, and not just for its old-school sensibilities about challenge. The sixteen sprawling levels you’ll blast your way through feature dizzying networks of shafts and chambers that make the most of your free-flight movement, just as the original Descent and its sequel did. But modern level design has been making places look like actual places for decades now, and Overload’s levels… don’t. As detailed as the auto-ops are and as luscious as the particle effects get, the rooms your battles rage in tend to be extremely plain. They never look like real, functional locales, just tunnels for you to hunt keys and secrets and robots in. Don’t get me wrong, they serve their purpose in their layout and complexity, but I have no doubt that a talented environment artist could have added details like catwalks and airlocks to make the levels feel lived-in and real.

Despite these missteps, Overload’s gameplay is some of the most hectic and gratifying you’ll get in the genre. Your weapons feel powerful and impressive as they shove auto-ops around and shatter them against the walls. Sparks, fire, and metal bits cascade through rooms with every robot you smash, making huge battles veritable typhoons of destruction. And for the explorers in the audience, you’ll have hundreds of secrets to turn up across the seven or eight hours it takes to blast through the campaign. There’s a challenge mode, New Game+, and even multiplayer that you probably shouldn’t count on being populated but hey, it’s there. Overload is the Descent revival we didn’t know we wanted, still a little stuck in the past but flashy and fun enough to make a solid shooter.

As a spiritual successor to Descent 1 & 2, Overload presents an interesting contrast to Descent 3. D3 brought a lot of innovation and experimentation, but with deeply mixed delivery. Overload, however, hews far closer to the formula established by D1 & D2, but with a thick sheen of polish. It's at once a joy to see a modern 6DOF executed so gracefully and a disappointment that its ambitions were so reigned in.

Credit where it's due, Overload isn't devoid of innovations on the first two Descents. They're clearly inspired by the double decades of FPS innovation between D2 and Overload, but they fit so snugly within Overload's design that they're still warmly welcomed. Upgrade points let you customize your weapons, keeping your arsenal fresh. Bite-sized audio-log storytelling smoothly layers over the action. Its challenge survival mode fits great (and should make a nice amuse-bouche between the main campaign and NG+/DLC campaign runs).

The lack of ambition are most felt in areas furthest from the core "shoot robots, destroy reactor, get out" Descent loop. The story, soundtrack, and level design are functional but mostly unmemorable. The art style also falls into this, only buoyed by the rendering tech ensuring a degree of visual appeal. (This is worst with the enemy design, which lacks much of any personality and makes many enemy types feel interchangeable.)

However, the degree of polish Overload exudes is really worth note. Every weapon has its use case, every enemy has their own way to challenge you, and damn if that classic Descent formula doesn't still work wonders. I can't even blame the developers too much for their limited artistic ambitions - publishing a 6DOF shooter in 2018 was ambitious enough as is. I'm still holding out hope that, someday, someone will take the 6DOF shooter genre to a place that isn't just flying spaceships to blow up robots & explode reactors. Until then, Overload is a good reminder that there's a reason people stick so close to the original formula - it still hits.

Simply put this is the best zero gravity shooter in recent years, and possibly in forever. --yes more games like it exist, but not very many, and this is absolutely the one you want to buy first. I would encourage new players to spend some time in the training level getting a feel for strafing up and down and rolling left and right, flying on their back -- any other sort of movement or orientation they can dream up... this sort of excersize not only helps get yourself used to the controls but will also help you navigate some of the more complex levels.

And complex some of these levels are.  The game provides you with a holographic guide robot you can activate at almost any time and will lead you from wherever you are to your next objective so you don't need to worry about getting lost if you go exploring.  The game does get punishingly hard as you get farther into it so dark souls fans should be in love. :P  Although there is no checkpoint system you can also save at almost any time.

Finally, there is a simple yet surprisingly deep plot going on as you make your way across the moons of saturn and beyond... It's presented as a sort of murder mystery and hooked me in even though I didn't think I was playing the game for its story at all.  You can tell the writer is a fan of Ender's Game and Agatha Christie since the story comes across as something like a mix of the two.  Even if you don't manage to find all the audio logs and background information you never feel lost in it, and it's remarkably well-written as well as being engaging.

So, even though the mission objectives can sometimes feel repetitive and the three bosses might be a *titch* too easy once you've wrapped your head around flying instead of walking, I still wholeheartedly, unreservedly recommend this game to anyone, not just fans of the old Descent titles.  It's an exhilarating experience that, if you've ever dreamed of flying and woken up feeling wistful, will never get old.

Lets start with the [b]Multiplayer first[/b].
Finding a match usually goes quite fast, max time i had to wait so far where about 5 minutes, ofc. it really depends on the time, especially during the hours where EU peeps head to bed and US peeps get home from work the multiplayer can be quite dry untill they all ate their dinner and are rdy to match up (wich is, the way live works, so not really a negative point)

The multiplayer matches themself are quite fun, i love the 1v1's since it reminds me alot of quake, ofc. the item spawns are random, but the player who keeps map control and item control (as random as they may be, this ones actually important) has the upper hand, aswell as knowing where ur enemy can come from, so skilled prefiring works just fine to get the headstart in a dodgefight.

The Anarchy matches (in other words, free for all) deliver alot of action, aswell as planning ahead, either u are that type of guy that goes straight into the action or the one that sneaks up behind of all that mess to try and snack a few kills.
And this game does contain "assists", so there is no real "kill stealing" since those "assists" give u points aswell (ofc. not as much as a solid kill) - this especially kept my frustration low haha :D
Same for the Team Anacrhy (TDM) , it can be really fun to play this in a 3v3 or 4v4, sticking to your teammates or spreading out to flanck the enemys.
Sadly i couldn't find any TDM without asking/gathering people in beforehand.

Next thing are the servers, there arent many available and me as EU player, i often see myself "forced" into USA servers, the netcode isn't too bad, but u feel the lag at around 150ms and people with 30ms ping have a clear advantage on you.
Gladly u can setup private matches, with your own set of rules and invite people to it, wich is also tons of fun.
The game does contain a matchmaking and ranking system, but as you can guess, matchmaking only works well when there are enough people playing at the same time - so it can happen, especially at those "empty" times ([i]see above[/i]) that a plat player gets qued up with a bronze or silver.

Time to check out the [b]Campaign[/b].
The story itself consists of Radiologs and Text, since theres quite alot of stuff going on it can take 2 playthroughs to really understand the story, since listening to those radiologs WHILE fighting a hord of bots isn't really the easiest thing to do.
But they deliver every reason to do the campaign twice because after your first runthrough u unlock the "NewGame+" where u keep all your upgrades and weapons from your first run through in addition to more and harder enemys, delivering you a real challenge.
The campaign itself is actually quite easy for most experienced 6dof players, it really comes down when u play it on harder difficulties - wich sure is challenging, but can sometimes just be straight out frustrating.
Keeping the difficulty high tho makes up for the repetitive objective *blowing up reactors, all day long*
Every 5 Levels u get to fight a boss, wich... sadly i found underwhelming so thats a minus from me.
The maps themself contain the well known secrets, switches, locked doors, secret levels etc. wich reward u with upgrade points wich u can invest into your ship after each level.
Now it really depends on what kind of player you are, but if u enjoy hunting secrets etc. for a 100% playthrough then this can keep u on your toes for a while.

Time for the [b]Challenge mode[/b].
This is by FAR my favorite time killer in the game, it is so much fun!
U got several maps to choose from, several difficulties and u can choose between countdown and infinity.
So why do i find it the most fun? Becouse i love to top the scores of the other pilots, especially when u can show off in their Discord :D
Infinity literally means that u try to survive a hord of bots as long as u can, the difficultie increases the longer u last.
The most fun part is countdown tho, u get 5 minutes to destroy as many bots as u can, as fast as you can and since it is only 5 minutes u start to tell yourself "just one more run, just one more run".

Due to the amount of configurations the [b]Options[/b] become their own part in my review!
At first it is overwhelming and superb confusing, escpeially for people who have no idea what mouse limiting does, or what tri-chord,allwas and hybrid means.
If u have problems with setting up your controls then i STRONGLY ADVICE that u head into their discord and ask the people!
It really helps out, i had my configuration set up after a few minutes and it feels spot on for m/kb.
It gives so many things u can change/tweak/play around with that u can literally set it up for dual joysticks, hotas, gamepads, probably even a steeringwheel with pedals - it's truely amazing!
You just need to take that time to set it up tho - but its worth the effort.

So all in all, the Campaign could have been a bit more - especially the bosses, but i did enjoy the extra challenge with my second and third playthrough on higher difficulties.
Aswell as gathering the achievments and finding the secrets.
So this part gets a 4/5 from me

The Multiplayer gets a 3/5 from me - it could have been more love, like a serverlist for example.
On the other hand, if the playercount rises just a bit more then i give it a 4/5 - becouse then it is garanteed to get big TDM matches up'n'going without having to gather people in discord.

Just the fact that i spend 80% of the playtime in Challenge-mode makes me give it a 5/5, it is still not boring and beating the top scores is so satisfying.

The options get a 3/5 from me, because i had my difficulties with them at first, not knowing what they exactly do - wich forced me to ask in their discord for help and advice.

All in all a 4/5 game for me :)

A glorious return to form by the kings of 6DoF shooters. It is impossible to overstate how much they nailed every detail, from movement (ship inertia, mouse acceleration), to level design, enemy variety, gunplay, and perhaps most of all, THE F🔥🔥🔥ING SOUNDTRACK.

Plays flawlessly on the Steam Deck.

Conceptually, Overload is a first-person tunnel shooter with no gravity, kind of like Doom except the floor and ceiling don't really matter. But at its heart, Overload really just seems to be about blowing stuff up.

It's an incredibly... well... crunchy game. A good selection of weapons, but not too many, all of which result in delightfully satisfying explosions when applied to the robotic minions you'll encounter around every corner. It's not the usual experience I expect from an indie developer, and it's really hard to get bored of.

On top of that, the campaign is pretty well-executed too. It's fairly long, but not too long - five to ten hours, probably, depending on your play style - and what seems like a fairly ho-hum plot at first began to draw my attention by the end. The minimalistic (but nonetheless voiced) cutscenes, briefings and in-game dialogue make the game's budget more obvious but they made good use of what they could afford.

Once you get to the end of that, if you're not done blowing stuff up, you can move into Challenge Mode, which is basically an endless zombie-survival kind of game where the objective is to score as high as possible and climb up the leaderboards, or multiplayer where you can choose between free-for-all, head-to-head and team game modes. Both options are considerably tougher than the main game, so I'd recommend tackling them later to most people - you'll need to have well-practiced 6DOF flying skills for best results.

Unfortunately, there is no co-operative multiplayer mode, at least not for the time being - that's probably the most glaring omission in Overload. A capture-the-flag mode might not have gone astray either. But there's still easily enough on offer for the game to be worth playing.

Overall - considering the spotty track record of indie/self-published games, the professionalism Revival displays in Overload is pretty remarkable. Even if 6DOF isn't your cup of tea, they've shown they're a studio worth watching in future.

The crew from the classic Descent games returns for a modern incarnation of the 6-degrees-of-freedom games we all know and love. There are three primary game modes available:

[h1]Single Player Campaign[/h1]
Much like the old-school shooters it draws influence from, the biggest draw in this game is easily the single player campaign. The Cronus Frontier campaign is no-nonsense, fast-paced action. While a little bit shorter compared to the classics of old, the overall level design and difficulty balance is much more polished. With five selectable difficulty levels, both directionally-challenged newbies and challenge-seeking veterans should be able to find some enjoyment here. The upgrade system offers a nice bit of flexibility to your playstyle and nicely rewards those with a keen eye for secrets. My only criticisms are that I found most of the boss fights to be somewhat underwhelming, and that some players might find the lack of mission variety to grow a bit repetitive by the end.

[h1]Challenge Mode[/h1]
Challenge Mode pits you into an arena with endlessly spawning bots, with two seperate sub-modes: Countdown (Get as many kills as possible in a 5-minute time limit) and Infinite (Survive as long as possible, getting as many kills as you can before being taken down). The item and enemy spawns are randomized on every playthrough to ensure that no two plays are the exact same. While this does keep the mode from getting stale, it is a bit of a double-edged sword for anyone looking to place high on the in-game leaderboards. Ranking up in that regard can often feel somewhat dependent upon randomly rolling a favorable intersection of high-value targets and strong powerup pickups. If you're not too worried about chasing leaderboards, though (or even if you are!), there's still quite a lot of fun to be had here once you've finished up the campaign.

[h1]Multiplayer[/h1]
Multiplayer is, much like the single player campaign, all about straightforward, no-nonsense action. Rules are simple - blow up the other guys, but don't get blown up yourself. First, the bad news - the multiplayer experience is currently considerably restrictive and laden with flaws. Long wait times, finnicky ranking system, squirelly lag compensation, lack of a server browser, and very limited number of servers all mean that getting a balanced match without frustrating hit-registration problems is unfortunately not something you can expect to get consistently. There's also a distinct lack of multiplayer co-op options available for the campaign and challenge modes.

The good news, though, is that the developers have stated that they are aware of these issues, and are looking to make improvements here one of their next focuses once the console versions are completed. Here's hoping we see improvements in the future.

At last a true heir to Descent in the 6DoF genre-space! Made by some of the people who created that classic, this game is so clearly just “more of that and better” that at times I worried they didn't have any new ideas; the setting is a gritty space future with teleportation and corporate overlords, where a mining company has created autonomous droids to do the work, then you come along and get pressed into fighting the “accidental” war machines when they go out of control and start killing people.

Yet they took all of that and mixed in a lot of modern style, from the smooth graphics to the faster-paced wave-shooter fun and time attack challenge maps. The level design is a bit simpler / more straightforward, though might just feel that way because the auto-maps are excellent. Side paths in the levels are more satisfying since they've been formalized, like Lockdowns where you destroy a group in a locked room, or the secret level teleport cubes sending you to tough challenge maps which don't punish dying and grant rewards for a certain number of kills.

I would also argue the upgrade tokens scattered around mission maps provide a better reward than a powerup you may not need. The upgrades can be spent between most levels in various ways like allowing you to hold more ammo, use less energy or increase flight speed. Some of the more high-stakes choices are super upgrades to weapons in which you take one of two exclusive paths, generally to emphasize a few traits of the weapon. As someone with not great aim, I appreciate how many of the weapons get homing with 1 or 2 upgrades. For those who are great at shooters, you often get more power when you don't pick the ease-of-use super upgrades.

The usual variety of weapons are all here, and mostly all feel different from each other. Primaries are split into 5 energy weapons and 3 bullet weapons, with both groups offering short and long range options so you can meet any situation no matter what ammo you have. The energy weapons get all the fun special powers such as wall bouncing or being able to charge. Secondary weapons with individual ammo tanks include floating orbs (perfect to fire past corners because they move toward nearby enemies) and a variety of missile pods (which feel great to spam-fire in quick bursts) plus the classic shrapnel bomb. Later toys do cool stuff like slow down time or pull enemies in.

Flight feels smooth and – after testing out various options in the control settings – keyboard and mouse control worked really well. Speaking of controls, make sure you've got something mapped as a Smash key. Though not explained perfectly, ramming smash attacks send your ship shooting forward for a decent amount of damage, and you get a little armor from the hit. Don't just try to boost toward enemies; you have to use the Smash.

Mission briefings and audio logs found around the maps all have excellent voice acting, telling a dramatic story about a control-hungry tech tycoon who thought Saturn could be remade into a new hub of space-faring civilization. As his dreams of a backwater empire crumbled, he became suspicious of everyone and demanded more security droids to protect his big secret. The ending to all of this gets even wilder than you might expect, with a chase across the universe after a man seeking immortality where you either save or doom humanity.

Beating the game unlocks New Game Plus with more enemies, randomized pickups and most of the upgrade tokens in the levels replaced with ammo. Basic upgrades are carried over and you start with every weapon, which allows you to try different super upgrades using the points gained from completing each map, destroying bosses and secret levels. Maybe this is from starting on medium difficulty but the foes feel smarter than in past 6doF games, doing things like dodging dumbfire rockets or ducking behind cover after taking a few shots.

When you don't feel like tackling a full mission or need a warmup before starting one, Challenge Maps throw you into a smaller survival map for five minutes or until you die. Weapons automatically upgrade and the XP gained throughout the game grants very necessary starting buffs. I love survival map gamemodes like this because they're often quick and easy fun, yet feel meaningful when attempting a new personal best – or in this case attempting the extra tough achievements. If I had the space to keep this game installed all the time, I would just for this mode.

This brings up one of the game's extremely minor flaws: the XP system feels bad early on when the challenge maps hurt without the starting buffs, then becomes meaningless later. Over in multiplayer, your XP also grants more starting options, punishing anyone who just wants to jump into that side. Perhaps that's a good reminder someone should play a while before attempting PvP, but it feels like a weird gate. They could have cut XP and locked the challenge map starting buffs another way.

Also, to my personal annoyance, Descent 2's wall panels are back. They still simply claim a door was unlocked when you shoot them and don't provide clues to where. Happily though, the panels are a lot more obvious now as big red buttons, while the linked doors are often close and no longer open just once.

Overall, if you liked Descent and want a modern mimic, or you like shooters and want to dive into the 6DoF genre, this game is great. Also strongly consider getting the DLC bundle; the soundtrack is awesome, the extra challenge maps are interesting and only sometimes buggy, while the two player-made campaigns are solid if slightly ordinary.

I'm not exaggerating when I say I believe Overload is the best old-school FPS released in a decade. Stellar large non-linear secret-laden level design, weapon variety balance, incredibly intuitive and customizable controls, intelligent enemy behavior and enemy variety come together to form a pure and action-fueled experience with no bullshit or long boring corridors between each fight.

Overload is not 'just' a Descent clone, it is also a refinement in many ways that makes it the ultimate 6DoF game. It's way more fair in how health items are placed, hitscan enemies are used tastefully, the Thief-Bot, Class 1 Driller or Red Hulk is no more in Overload, the difficulty overall is more balanced, robot generators are destroyable, and reactor rooms can no longer be cheesed. Even on the higher difficulties you can just dogfight enemies in a fun way rather than having to hide behind corners and take potshots so you don't die. The new Smash Attack, where you ram into enemies directly with your ship, even recovers a bit of health so you can get more aggressive. 

It features an upgrade system, but unlike other games where you end up with every upgrade in the game towards the end, here you need to make a permanent decision between two upgrade branches for each weapon, each of which augments the weapon in a different way, but you can't have both. Kind of like augs in the original Deus Ex. This way you actually have to weigh your options and decide which one suits you the best, giving you more replay value for future playthroughs if you want to try something different, as opposed to providing you with an illusion of choice where you'll get everything eventually, and the only choice there is is what upgrade you want first. Upgrade points are mostly found through secrets, so you really want to explore as much as you can.

There is an actual story this time around, mostly told by intro briefings and finding audio logs scattered around the levels, but the logs themselves are very short so they don't get too intrusive, and the story never forces you through unskippable cutscenes or forced walking(/flying?) sections where you can't do anything. You can pretty much disable it all in the options menu.

It features a functional multiplayer mode which usually has about 10 or 20 people playing it as of writing, but don't really expect it to get really populated outside of finding matches on the Discord. Do expect that you will get your ass kicked by Descent veterans who have been playing its multiplayer for over 20 years. 

The passage of time has allowed Overload to improve its visuals over Descent in many ways. Bots explode in chunky debris and hellfire. Kill an enemy by ramming into him and his corpse is sent flying across the map. Dynamic lighting makes the dark cavern areas much more tense to fight in. Robot eyes flicker when they take damage, and they light up to indicate more strongly they're being damaged. The particle effects enemies like the Shredder give off makes them even more menacing. The only unfortunate part is that the texturing and the colors used for the levels themselves makes them stand out much less from eachother.

Even though this game runs on the Unity Engine, it is remarkably well optimized, and save for certain shaders I experienced next to no framedrops on a medium system.

If you call yourself an FPS fan and are also anticipating the full release of other old-school FPS throwbacks such as DUSK, Ion Maiden and Amid Evil, do yourself a favor and get Overload. If you completed the game once, you can try it again on New Game+ with revamped enemies where late-game enemies appear much earlier on to shake things up.

An excellent continuation of the original Descent games, 20-some years into the future.

The graphics are quite pretty and have a pleasant aesthetic, the movement feels very, very rewarding and has a great sense of speed and momentum when you boost down a hall, then duck into a side passage or down a shaft. Mouselook is very well implemented and has no real hard turning cap.

Combat feels great as all weapons and missiles have good audio and visual feedback. You can feel the force of impact and it just feels good.

The levels are spacious and well designed, you would sometimes get a little lost but it's nothing too horrible and you have a holo bot to guide you to your next objective, if you need it.

Multiplayer works surprisingly well. The community is tight but you can always count on the matchmaking finding you an opponent, even if it's just you two queueing, which is great. The multi maps are fun and varied in size and style.

Oh, I almost forgot. LEVEL EDITOR! This is basically half the reason I bought the game.

Overall, an easy, solid recommendation for anyone who likes first person combat and the freedom of movement that this sub-genre offers!
