[h1]Overview[/h1]
Overload is a first-person spaceship shooter set indoors with an emphasis on freedom of movement, secret finding, and combat. 

[b]The Good[/b]
[list]
[*] Secrets
[*] Soundtrack
[*] Challenge modes
[*] Weapon and ship upgrades
[*] Pathing guidance
[/list]
[b]The Bad[/b]
[list]
[*] Difficulty
[*] Forced weapon swapping
[*] Secrets in timed level sections
[*] Powerup locations
[*] Blocked upgrading
[/list]
[b]Buy or Try[/b]
[list]
[*] Buy on sale or seek an alternative
[/list]
[b]Stability[/b]
[list]
[*] No crashes, graphical anomalies, or sound issues
[*] Frame rate drops encountered noticeably in later areas
[*] My System: Windows 10, i7-7700 @ 3.60GHz, 16GB ram, 1060 3GB, played at 1920 x 1080
[/list]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
In Overload you control a spacecraft within mining facilities on Saturn's moons. You'll fight your way to rescue captives, destroy reactors, and then escape before they explode. The game's 16 levels are labyrinthine interior environments full of cramped spaces and variable lighting. Navigation is aided by a hologram wayfinder, automap, flares, and headlights. These tools will prove useful as you'll need to explore thoroughly for weapons, energy, armour pickups, audio logs, security keys, and upgrade points used to buff your weapons and ship between missions. Rescuing captives is optional though provides rewards and impacts the game's ending. 

Your 16 weapons are split evenly into two groups. Primary weapons are your main guns ranging from gattling lasers to flak cannons. Secondary weapons are explosives ranging from missile launchers to time-slowing bombs. Separate weapon wheels for each group makes for convenient swapping. All weapons have two tiers of upgrades, the second of which is a choice between two options. For instance, you could opt to improve your missiles' homing ability or instead go for a straight damage boost. Enemies vary in their own weapons and maneuverability posing ever-greater threats. In addition to standard foes are three boss battles spread evenly across the campaign. 

Story is delivered between missions and during play with additional details found within collectible audio logs. The game provides quicksaving and manual saving, with no in-level autosaving (that I'm aware of). Overload includes a campaign, newgame+, multiplayer (not reviewed), and two challenge modes. Challenge mode is a series of 12 separate maps to destroy as many enemies as possible either within a 5 minute window or as long as you can survive. XP earned from killing foes in all single-player offerings go towards permanent ship upgrades in challenge mode. Weapons in challenge mode are levelled up from scratch each time you play a round. 

An uptempo soundtrack complements the action. Overload includes 50 Steam Achievements with the majority attained by less than 1% of players. In a little over 16 hours I beat the campaign on the 3rd of 5 difficulty options as well tried most of the challenge mode maps.

[h1]Critique[/h1]
Midway through the campaign I was having a blast but upon beating it was left underwhelmed and disappointed. A good first impression made me willing to overlook a misstep or two. But the further I got the more problems arose to the extent they could no longer be ignored. The freedom of movement, the combat, and the majority of the level design was well executed. Hunting for secrets was just as fun as winning battles with both offered in equal measure. Though I amassed a series of minor gripes what killed my enjoyment was a lack of consistency and, more glaring, an unfairly balanced difficulty.

Upgrade points are mainly found in secret areas, a design I've hated since 1997's Jedi Knight forced secret hunting to improve Force powers. That said Overload is a lesser offender, for though it's doubtful you'll locate every secret you'll still find enough to upgrade all the things you'll actually use. During my run I was able to upgrade my mainstay weapon to maximum, all of my ship upgrades, as well as most of my preferred secondary weapons. Annoyingly, around mission 9 you'll lose your ability to upgrade entirely, despite the fact you'll still be acquiring new weapons. 

Like in the campaign, when you level up your weapons in challenge mode you are granted a choice between two options. Unfortuntaely the options aren't described, instead referred to with generic names like Missiles XL. Lacking a Codex to review upgrade options you won't have a clue what you are choosing. Since enemy and weapon descriptions are often provided before campaign levels I found the lack of a Codex strangely absent.

All of your secondary weapons have their own ammo counts and you'll use them all. Primary weapons don't have ammo that is collected, but rather that is pulled from one of two of your HUD's status bars. This was confusing, something I only figured out for myself after beating the campaign, reading the manual, then going back to play around some more. Some weapons use energy while others use "ammo" represented by the white bar. You won't need to swap primary weapons since enemies don't have particular weaknesses and most fights will be fought in a confined space. Because of this, slow firing weapons are terrible. My preferred weapon was energy based and energy is in great supply. Frankly I feel the white status bar could have been removed.

Secondary weapons are the most inventive yet some are lackluster with others downright annoying. The Vortex is one of the last acquired yet barely deals any damage. The Time Bomb is the worst offender as it literally slows things to a crawl. Three time-limited powerups can also be found consisting of a weapon boost, invulnerability, and cloak. These work fine but not when placed in a secret area you'll never locate when beset upon by enemies when entering a new location.

Overload's biggest issue is that it is less about skill and more about managing saves. Without autosaves you'll rely on quicksaving, and should you not make additional manual saves at high health, you can find yourself in unwinnable situations. Certain level sections make avoiding damage impossible, such as when you are locked or teleported into a small room surrounded by enemies. These moments are made worse by the fact that found health pickups are finite. I'd often quicksave with less than 100 armour expecting to find a boost later on, only to instead be thrust into a confined space where enemies would destroy me in seconds before I could get my bearings.

Enemy spawn stations and wall turrets that can't be destroyed, secrets tied to time-limited escapes, and forced weapon swapping to open doors can all be attributed to poor design choices in what I initially thought was a really good game. And don't get me started on the story. Oh, a virus has turned autonomous machines against the crew of an expensive mining outpost? Rather than just save the crew and destroy the machines, blow the station up too. That makes perfect sense.  

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
The level design is good. The soundtrack is apt. And the challenge modes make for quick and fun combat. In light of its problems I can only recommend it on sale. Should you buy it, take my advice. Set the difficulty to Rookie, don't obssess over every secret, find a weapon that works for you, and make manual saves too. EVERSPACE and Sublevel Zero Redux offer similar combat with more consistent design and can often be found at a discount. I would have been happier had Overload been outright bad. It nails some of the hardest things to do right. I'm saddened by how little it would have taken to transform my frustration into complete and utter delight.

[list]
[*] "Decent" - instead of "Descent," get it?
[/list]

Regarding World-Scale and VR:

1.
100% scale is unnaturally large on the Valve Index...(a cockpit sized for a giant; robot-monstrosities; etc)...I highly recommend reducing scale by at least 20% ( I prefer 60%).

(SteamVR -> Settings -> Video -> Per Application -> Overload).

2.
If you've already lost your ability to experience discomfort in VR, try disabling the cockpit...it improves both gameplay and performance.

3.
Nearly all in-game Graphical settings can be reduced to minimum without fundamentally altering image quality.

…just keep the following settings one step above the lowest tier:

"Shadows"

"Effects Lighting"

"Texture Resolution"

"Post-Processing"

*Anisotropic Filtering (negligible performance cost)

*Screen Space Reflections (negligible performance cost)

**Reduced Shaders**
Enemy cloaking causes a spontaneous performance drop in some Arenas...the reduced shader setting appears to prevent this by disabling the effect on some maps, but it also reduces the quality of dynamic lighting for sparks/explosions.

4.
Weak CPUs may choke in specific sections of a map due to the to the aggressive/sloppy automatic culling used in the game. Just keep that in mind and/or stay a certain distance away from certain fans, etc.

I once had a dream about a modern Descent game. That dream is now a reality. 

This is the game the Descent fans have been waiting for and even though it doesn't have the Descent name, it does have its developers and that is what matters. The game doesn't only feel good, it feels better than Descent. The weapons feel impactful and strong, the robots are menacing and provide quite a challenge. Overload has 5 main difficulty levels with one extra "secret" difficulty. The different difficulties make sure that a wide variety of players with different skill levels can have a fun and fairly challenging time. 

The single player campaign levels we've had a chance to play in early access have been very promising. In addition to the classic Descent style mine clearing and secret hunting, there is now an upgrade system, so your playthroughs can actually vary a fair bit depending on which types of weapon and ship upgrades you choose to specialise in.

The visuals in this game are great. The modern game engine allows for some very impressive visual effects which truly bring the game alive and make it very atmospheric. The lighting in particular is great. Firing a flare down a dark cave system or seeing a robot's headlight coming around a corner in a dark tunnel is truly something special.

Overload also comes with two "challenge modes". "Infinite" is essentially a last stand survival mode. Robots keep spawning and you have to survive for as long as possible while destroying as many robots as possible. "Countdown" has a 5 minute timer, destroy as many bots as you can and try to survive until the end. Once the 5 minutes runs out, your ship blows up and it's game over. Both modes have online leaderboards, so there is definitely a competetive aspect to it. The modes do have some luck-based elements such as powerup spawns. If you get a bunch of invulnerability powerups, you're most likely going to score higher. Such elements can be quite frustrating for the really competitive players. Overall the challenge mode is a very fun experience where you can really push your limits.

Finally there's the Multiplayer. Currently there are two game modes Anarchy and Team-anarchy, essentially deathmatch and team-deathmatch. Weapons are altered from their single player counter-parts for balance reasons.

Multiplayer beta plays really quite well as long as you have low ping. Currently the multiplayer uses official matchmaking servers that are in different parts of the world. The servers seem to be good quality and connected to the German server I got ping ranging from 30-50 while connecting from Estonia with a 100/100 Mbps connection. To the North American East Coast server my ping was 120-140 and West Coast was 180-200.

Overall this game is definite recommend for me. If you liked the Descent games, I'm sure you'll have a blast with this.

Do you all remember the scene in the film [i]Ratatouille[/i] when Anton Ego, the restaurant critic, took his first bite of the ratatouille which instantly triggered flashbacks to his childhood when he ate the same dish his mother cooked for him? This happened to me with [i]Overload[/i], and it will happen for many of you who have experienced the [i]Descent[/i] series as a kid (or as an adult too 😊).

I remember loading up [i]Overload[/i] for the first time, and it triggered the memory of my dad buying my first new computer when I was 9 years old: a Compaq Presario 9232. It had three games: [i]Hardball 4[/i], [i]Magic Carpet[/i] (RIP Bullfrog), and [i]Descent: Destination Saturn[/i]. I remember loading up [i]Descent[/i] for the first time and could not move at all. I was used to using the arrow keys for games. So I was just rotating my ship around, shooting the destructible signs, and thinking when are the bad guys going to come? Embarrassingly, it took me about a week (after finally reading the manual), that you move forward and backwards using A and Z. Once I held that A button and heard that first scream from the Class 1 Drone, I knew I was in for a real treat. My dad rarely bought me games because he was worried about game violence (e.g. [i]Doom[/i]), but he knew [i]Descent[/i] was more family-friendly. Over the years, he gave me [i]Descent: Anniversary Edition[/i] (which I didn’t realize until I got the game that the campaign had me going past Saturn), [i]Descent 2: Infinite Abyss[/i], and [i]Descent 3[/i]. Prior to [i]Descent 3[/i] coming out, I convinced my dad to get me a PC with a graphics card since [i]Descent 3[/i] required one. He agreed, and my new PC came equipped with an S3 Savage4 card. Although it was a budget card, I was able to experience the final chapter of the Material Defender.

Subsequently, I was following rumors and possible concept art for [i]Descent 4[/i], then hearing [i]Descent 4[/i] being cancelled, then reading that Interplay was bankrupt, and then Interplay sort of re-emerging which gave some hope that the series might revive again. Nearly 20 years later, the original creators of [i]Descent[/i] created its own company, [i]Revival Productions[/i], to develop the long-awaited spiritual successor of [i]Descent[/i].

I was bummed that I missed the Kickstarter for the game, but I cannot imagine the anxiety of the developers during those last 24 hours. I wish I knew about the game to help out at the time. So, thank you for all the Kickstarter backers for making this game happen! I know if the developers start another Kickstarter project (e.g. [i]Freespace 3[/i]… fingers crossed!), then I will definitely contribute knowing how well [i]Overload[/i] was developed and produced. Thank you to the Revival team for allowing me to relive my childhood memories and congratulations for producing a fantastic game!

Many reviewers have already gone into the features of the game, but I would like to reiterate that there are many types of gameplay that fits everyone’s needs and extends the replayability and life of the game. It’s not just a [i]Descent[/i] game with modern graphics. There’s the single player campaign with a deeper storyline and voice acting. In addition, there is your arcade-like Challenge Mode that would likely bring hours and hours of gameplay to get to the top of the leaderboard. Then there is the multiplayer to challenge other pilots in anarchy and team anarchy with more multiplayer modes coming in the future. Lastly, there is the Level Editor that will be released shortly after [i]Overload’s[/i] release day that would bring on countless customization.

[h1]Welcome back 1998[/h1]

Ahh 6dof, how I've missed thee.  Since the days I was running Kali in Dos with a 14.4k modem, I've been playing descent online.  I took a long break, as did many others over the years.  Went to different games.  Got hooked on Overwatch for the last 2 years (600 hours on Reinhardt) but lately, it's been a struggle.  I was then hit with an epiphany, it's the game.

Multiplayer in Overload is a completely different vibe.  Overwatch gets frustrating, because usually when you lose it's your knucklehead team mates.  In Overdrive, [b]YOU ARE ONLY RESPONSIBLE FOR YOURSELF[/b].  When you lose or do poorly in Overdrive, you end up admiring your opponents skills and techniques.  There's nobody else to blame but you.  Everyone types "GG" after a game.  

[b] a primer on 6dof[/b]

6dof stands for "Six Degrees of Freedom".  In most shooters, you run along the ground, and point your gun at people.  6dof games offer something substantially different.  The ability to rise from the ground and move in any direction.   Probably the closest thing that can describe it would be First person drones, but in a zero-g environment.

[b] Gameplay[/b]

The pre-release game contains both single player campaigns, and if you ask nicely from various sources, a multiplayer component.  In 2 days of this review, it will be included in the release. In addition to these game modes, there's also a "Challenge Mode" where wave after wave of enemies with ever increasing difficulty come after you. 

You fly a small spaceship that's equipped with a variety of main weapons, that come in 2 flavors, energy and ballistic.  The ammo for either can be used on a fairly nice spectrum of guns.  You have plain lasers, a charge laser, shotgun, flak.   On the secondary side you have missiles or bombs.  Missile pods are small missiles with rudimentary tracking.  Hunters are full homing.  There's also a time bomb that in campaign or challenge mode creates bullet time, slowing down the gameplay giving you crucial time to lay some robots to waste.

[b]Controls[/b]

Developers did a fantastic job capturing the feel of the original descent.  This is probably the most important aspect of this game is the controls.  There's a lot of things you have to turn off to get the original trichord control style, but it's in there.  The controls menu offers a plethora of mappable controls, and even an analog axis recalibration tool.   Very very nice.  I can't talk this up enough.

[b]Multiplayer[/b]

This is really what it's all about, and will make or break any game these days.  Multiplayer will be harder for newcomers, because a lot of the people playing this game have been playing similar games since 98' (Wow, 20 years!)  but if you're up for a challenge, this game has already gotten the seal of approval from all these old 6dof "pilots" I'm no top tier, but even when I lose like I said above, nobody gets mad.  

There's a total of 3 modes for multiplayer.  Team vs Team, 1 VS 1, and deathmatch.  All of these modes are fairly self explanatory.  

I do find some critique with the multiplayer though.   The original gamebrowser in Descent 2 was great.  Joining games in progress that had no time limit was great too.  Not really a fan of the queuing system, but for all intents and purposes it works.

[b]Graphics[/b]

Very nice.  Sparks fly out of damaged robots, and when things die there's a giant explosion of sparks flying everywhere.  It's sort of like watching the death star blow up. Settings will allow you to do everything from run your graphics card cool, to cooking breakfast on it.

[b]Overall[/b]
5 out of 5.  A game like this hasn't been made in a while, and it's every bit the successor to the game that inspired it.  If you've never tried a 6dof game, start here.  If you're an old Descent Pilot looking for a new place to hang your helmet, hang it here.  Everyone from the old days are here.

[h] Overload - Not Just a Modernized Descent Game [\h]

Overload brings back the six degrees of movement tunnel games like Descent 1/2/3 and Forsaken. However, the development team went far beyond just the nostalgia of the past, they created a game that represents a near perfect 6DOF game. Through out the development, the dev team listened closely to the community and kickstarter donaters to create a game that shows how much passion the dev team has for this game. I believe you will be hard pressed to find another title that has this much direct support and community. While many dev teams disappear after release, you can still find the dev team actively interacting with the community through their discord channel, forums and weekly streams on twitch. The devs also run weekly challenges that will keep you engaged well beyond the standard play through.

The gameplay in Overload is amazing and whether you play on a gamepad, joystick or mouse you will find highly customizable settings that will allow you to find your perfect playstyle. This is especially true for mouse players, something D1/D2 did very poorly. So if you were a previous Descent player that used a Joystick, you might find you can easily play with a mouse and keyboard combo.

In the previous 6DOF freedom games you only had the ability to play either the single player mode of multiplayer modes, Overload introduces a new mode called Challenge Mode. In Challenge Mode you will be put against an ever increasingly difficult set of bots. The more bots you kill, the number of  bots increase and the harder they get. During the run, every so often super bots will spawn as your  number of kills increases. You will also be awarded weapon upgrades to ensure you can keep up with the ever increasing horde of bots You can play in either infinite mode, where you play until you die or timed mode, which challenges you to kill as many bots as possible in a set time limit. Challege mode also requires you to pay attention to your ammunition levels and make every shot count. If you don't you will be frantically flying around with no way to kill the bots. Leader boards are present for all levels and difficulties so you can let the world see just how good you are. Challange mode is also a great way to hone your flying skills in preparation for multiplayer madness.

Another new feature is the ability to customize your ship. Instead of being forced to find upgraded weapons, you can now select any weapon and missile setup, with the exception of the rare super weapons that spawn randomly during gameplay. You can also select ship perks that allow you to modify several aspects of your ship to further improve your flying style. While these customizations might make you think there is a perfect setup, I guarantee you they don't, The dev team really spent a lot of time balancing the weapon sets to ensure there is no one setup. This is especially fun for multiplayer where you can select two different ship setups that will ensure you have the right weapon types for the varied levels. Gone are the days of starting with a weak old pea shooter and frantically running around looking for a weapong upgrade. Instead, you are immediately a threat as soon as you spawn. This keeps the multiplayer games fun and furious.

Multiplayer offers three different modes. Anarchy, all against all. team mode and 1v1 . You can either queue for a game or setup a private passworded session so you can always team up with your friends. The private sessions are especially fun because it allows you to customize almost every features of the game. This includes changing the win conditions, levels, weapons and several other items. Multiplayer also supports optional setting for cross platform play. This provides a larger number of players to keep the action going. The level design are some of the best maps I have ever seen for this style of game. The will have you changing your ship loadouts to be effective in the session. Since you can pick two different loadouts, you will always have the right setup for the map type. You are also able to change from each setup during the gameplay so you will always be prepared. Overload also released a map editor which will ever increase the number of levels to play on. Revial Productions has published tutorials on how to use the tools so it is easy to get started.

Like most modern games Overload uses a queuing system to search for a session. While you can still ensure play with your friends using the private game setting, the regular queue requires you to wait for other players to join the queue. This means if no players are online, you will be stuck staring at a search screen until someone else joins in. There is no way to see how many people are currently online so you could be staring at the search screen for a long time. You can use the discord channel to try and find folks to play with, but this requires you to install another application to find a game and relies on other players to do the same. You are also unable to select the region you are playing in which can heavily impact your ping times. This dramatically changes your gameplay experience and can often leave you frustrated. Another area missing is the ability to join games currently in session, or immediately restart a session once the session timer expires forcing you to rejoin the queue. Since the queue has a session timer you may be stuck with only 1 other player. Ypu can host your own server, but this option is only available for local LAN play. This concerns me because this service requires Revival Productions to pay for the hosting, and without continual passive income, online play will go away. It is however important to note that the inital Kickstarter campaign did not include multiplayer as a feature. The dev team really pushed hard to get this feature in and shows just how much they love this game and their commitment to the community. The dev team is also actively engaged with the community to improve the online play so some of the issues may be resolved in the future.

To sum it up, I love this game and encourage you to try it. The graphics are amazing, the maps are varied and you can also play in VR mode giving you a whole new immersive experience. Former Descent players I promise you will feel right at home and be dog fighting in some of the best levels I have played. if you have never played a 6DOF game, I encourage you to the best game I have played in the 6DOF genre. With the release of the level editor, you are also ensured to have new caverns to explore that will keep the gameplay fresh.

The other reviews are impeccable at describing this game. The single word: Descent. Those familiar with that game will feel at home with this one. Majority of the changes between this and Descent are positive, and I'm not only talking about aesthetics. Sound effects have the right amount of crunch to them. Enemies are easy to spot and the improved graphics aren't intrusive to the experience. The physics of the ship are as tight as the spiritual predecessor and the weapons...the WEAPONS!

The weapons really show off the innovation of what could be done in a repetitive shooter market. Many of these weapons draw inspiration (or are blatant rips) from Luke's previous 2D Dual Stick shooter, Inferno (which is great in its own right). Many weapons are ingenious and extremely useful, like the Creepers and the Reflex (especially when fully upgraded). Others are clearly taken directly from Descent in form and function, like the Thunderbolt (Fusion) and the Impulse (Laser). There are weapons for different playstyles. Enjoy close quarters? Use the Crusher or Cyclone. Prefer to play it safe from a distance or aren’t too accurate with your shots? Use the Reflex, Missile Pods, or Hunters. Are you actually accurate with your shots? Use Falcons and the Driller. Another added layer is the upgrade system. It is a welcome addition and definitely good at empowering your weapons. It takes a little time to get used to, but once you do, you’ll be scouring maps for precious upgrade points to upgrade your favorite weapons. Want old fashions Quad Lasers? Done. Gauss or Vulcan Cannon? You’re set. Every weapon feels like it fits into a different niche and has its own purpose except maybe the Time Bomb (except when fully upgraded) and the Flak Cannon…which to be fair, I haven’t given enough time to try.

The level design is phenomenal. You’ll find yourself crawling through levels that twist and turn in every direction that even the auto-map gets confusing. Every inch of each map is teeming with encounters. The only critique I have here is that a lot of the areas have a samey feel. Maybe it’s just the nostalgia goggles, but I miss the elemental themed levels (as cliché as they might be) from the classic games. While comparing a game like this really isn’t fair, it still doesn’t help that I can’t visually tell if I was in Titan Collider or Phoebe. Of course, the ending levels are very far placed from the rest of the game so you get a good amount of variance there.  Additionally, in this game, I feel that enemies can be a bit repetitive so that you’re used to the same Harpies, Gorgons, Wyverns…and the darn Golem/Reavers. Other than that, the ship design looks like a flying toaster and customization is fairly simple. I also wish that pressing Esc would fast forward so you can see all the text for cutscenes instead of skipping the cutscene altogether.

And that’s it. Those 4 minor gripes are the only things that bother me about this game. Just about everything else is amazing. This game fits like a glove when you get the controls right, the difficulty is great, the level design is great, and the weapons are the best. Definitely recommend this for anyone interested in skill based combat in an old-new genre of shooter. 9/10 in my book :)

[h1]'Descent' into Ymir, Titan, Enceladus and beyond.[/h1]
[u][b]Premise:[/b][/u] In 2118, you'll operate a multi-purpose service vessel (MPSV) donned the “Iberia” registered to the Cronus Frontier which is a subsidiary of Juno Offworld Automation.

You, the ostensibly [i]unnamed[/i] pilot, will awaken and be contacted by an AI named “Mara” onboard the Iberia. Mara informs the pilot that an outpost on Ymir, a moon of Saturn, has had its operators — what are mining and security drones in the facility —  malfunction and become hostile. During the mission, the pilot learns more about the tumultuous relationship between Juno Offworld Automation and the Cronus Frontier CEO, Gabriel Kantor.

The story is exclusively told through preamble voiced text before each mission as well as audio logs found throughout the levels. The voice acting is quite good. Anecdotally, Overload feels a bit like System Shock, Red Faction and Perfect Dark 64 if they were all combined and re-imagined as a 6DOF game. Of course, this game actually made by the same devs as “Descent” under a different banner — appropriately named “Revival Productions”. Chiefly, Matt Toschlog, Mike Kulas of Parallax Software (now called Deep Silver Volition) and Luke Schneider of Radian Games.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
[i]Most[/i] level objectives are straightforward and.... unchanging. Typically revolving around very light exploration to find security keys, then going through the subsequent security door and destroying the main reactor. That or destroying a boss — then escaping. On occasion, you'll run into lockdown sectors that you need to destroy the subsequent security in order to leave , other objectives might include destroying a smaller reactor to de-power a security gate. Nearing the end however, this slightly changes. For narrative reasons, you need to pass through portals after supplying them with enough power. All without the aid of your holo-guide.

The game does not take place in “outer space” so much as it's inside of outposts and facilities around the moons of Saturn. A sort of “tunnel shooter”.

If you're unfamiliar with what “6DOF” means, it essentially means you've got full control of pitch, yaw and roll movements of the ship. “6 degrees of freedom”. A number of movement aids are available if you're easily disoriented, such as auto-roll — this can be augmented to the degree of which it is active with both strafing and mouse movement adjustments. 

6DOF games require a bit more spatial awareness than a traditional shooter. For instance the sight-lines are different, were this Call of Duty or Battlefield, you'd be able to reasonably predict where an enemy may appear around of the corner — being filled with ground-faring creatures. Even in something like CoD: Advanced Warfare or Titanfall, you can make a reasonable prediction that enemies' center of mass will appear just above the ground but not so high that your aim is perpendicular to the to the ground. Otherwise, a rough estimate can be made where a player could reasonably be wall running. In Overload/Descent, or in any 6DOF game for that matter, anything could be anywhere.

However, if you get lost, you can assign the holo-guide to track specific things on the map. Need more power? Tell it to guide you to an energy center. You can't overcharge there, but it can get you out of a bind. Have no idea where to go next? Tell to it to guide you to the next security key/gate. This of course only works in facilities assigned to Cronus Frontier.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2631696831

There are enemies in which their first parameter for attack is simply ramming into you — occasionally they will attempt this in a relatively furtive way. You'll be exploring for secrets, power-ups or what have you and all of a sudden this big metal beast will smack you on the side knocking you around.   With the clank of your metallic hull combined with the antagonistic engine sounds and the operators make, this surreptitious ramming can make you feel rather vulnerable — especially if you already feel uncomfortable with ideas like there not really being an up or down.

[h3]Misc[/h3]
Operators break up nicely. You can see them ignite from the inside and become inactive, ultimately sending them careening to their demise. Recognizing when they go inactive can save you a fair amount of ammo.

You can find upgrade points throughout stage. Used to increase stats like maximum ammo or damage from specific weapons.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2631686786

There's a challenge mode with its own separate unlocks and progression. But there is an NG+ after the campaign is completed.

Headlights draw small amount of power, which is acts as health underneath the shields. So it behooves one to use flares instead. They can also help reveal clocked operator positions — plus they look really cool.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2631686770

There's also cross-platform multiplayer, though I would not suspect it's very active.

Weapon variety is pretty decent. Everything from standard lasers and missiles to time bombs — and I don't mean a bomb with a timer, I mean a bomb that slows down time itself. There's also chain guns like the Cyclone that increase its rate of fire the longer the trigger is held, creeper mines that slowly seek out operators among many others.

[h3]The Gist[/h3]
It's a very fun, fast-paced and challenging shooter — especially on higher difficulties. There's not a lot of variation in the level design or mission objectives, which can be a real bummer. The story is actually pretty intricate and compelling, that is, if you actually pay attention to the mission briefs. Personally, I would wait for a sale, as I don't think what is here will satisfy people that are not actively seeking out a modern replacement for Descent.

Overload is a Six Degrees of Freedom first person shooter with a single player story mode, replayable challenge modes with leaderboard, and online multiplayer.  If you enjoyed Descent, you will enjoy this.  But why?  What about this game is special?

1) The Nostalgia

The moment you teleport into Ymir Outpost and start moving around, you already begin to recall the feeling of the original series.  The first secret you discover.  The first robot that pops out of a secret room after you trigger it.  The first time a Scorpion surprises you.  The first cryotubes you rescue.  The first secret level you find.  You will remember everything you loved about the original game as you get introduced to some of the new concepts that Overload brings to the table.

2) The Music

Much of the music of this game comes from Descent music legends Dan Wentz and Allistar Brimble.  You'll hear styles from Descent 1 and 2 as you play through the game.  But can we talk about Descent 3's Jerry Berlongieri and his absolutely brilliant "Unmanned", the soundtrack to level 14?  If there's nothing that gets me, it's music that fits what's going on.  Kantor's descent into madness is captured perfectly by this soundtrack, which starts making you, the player, start questioning reality.

3) The Story

The story starts out with you investigating various accidents that happened.  As you learn more, you start to feel that things are wrong.  This culminates in the level 15 mission briefing, AKA the "Three Queens" story.  Everything is PERFECT about this.  Not only does this briefing explain everything up to that point, it invokes a level of terror that you'd expect from rounding the corner into a Scorpion.  The voice acting on this part is exceptional as well, sends chills up and down the spine.

4) Challenge Modes

And after the story campaign, you can keep playing more with the addictive challenge modes.  12 maps teeming with robots for you to destroy and set high scores on the leaderboards.  Try to play as long as you can with infinite, or see how fast you can kill things on countdown mode.  It's a simple idea that players love.

While I can't help but glow about the single player experience, the multiplayer experience isn't quite as good.  This is largely because multiplayer wasn't intended to be part of the 1.0 release.  However, the team at Revival pivoted and decided to add multiplayer to this mix late.  This really shows in the disparity between in polish between single player and multiplayer.  While it might be difficult to justify criticizing the game for including something that it wasn't planning on, it is no longer Early Access, and needs to be looked at as such.

There are a number of missing features with multiplayer: co-op campaign compatibility, server browsing, joining games in progress, hosting dedicated servers, Hoard CTF & Monsterball game modes that were popular in Descent 3, and a way to observe games in progress (my #1 feature request).  It really seems like multiplayer is something that either should have delayed the release of 1.0, or should have been part of a 2.0 release several months down the line.  It is not great that multiplayer was released half-or-less-finished.

For playing multiplayer itself, you're forced into playing client-server.  There are no peer to peer options, which means that a 50ms swing in ping can be the difference between winning 9-8 and losing 11-20 against the same pilot, just because you had different pings on different servers.  The lower your ping, the more what you see is accurate, which means you get a pretty big advantage over someone who is at a higher ping.

Anarchy has a strange points system that rewards 3 points for a kill and 1 point for an "assist", which requires you to do a certain amount of damage right before someone else gets the kill.  I very still much believe anarchy should just be based on kills, because now you get situations where games end because someone with 18 kills and 6 assists win over someone with 19 kills and 2 assists.

Don't let this get you totally down about multiplayer.  The actual multiplayer games can be quite fun, and as long as you can deal with these nitpicks, you'll still have a good time.  No other game outside of the Descent series has a multiplayer that can even be called comparable to that series, so Overload at least has that going for them.

The other thing that Overload has going for them is their exceptional and responsive dev team (edit: See below for update).  All those multiplayer nitpicks I discussed above?  They're *working* on resolving some of them, and are very good at listening to player feedback when determining what to tackle next.  I feel confident knowing that this game will continue to evolve, especially remembering where the closed beta of multiplayer was a month prior to release, and how far it has come since.  (Spoiler alert: It was *terrible* back then.)

So if you're looking for an authentic Six Degrees of Freedom single player experience that brings the genre into modern times, I can't recommend this game enough.  It even supports both Individual Level and full game speedrunning, has a new game+ mode where the levels change up to add even more difficulty, and has a ton of replayability.  Multiplayer feels unfinished, but give it a shot, and if you're not happy with what you see yet, don't be surprised if in an update down the road you see something added that you wanted in the game.

[edit]
I wanted to edit this review because eight months on from release, and not a whole lot has changed with multiplayer.  The main nitpicks are still there.  There've been some weapon balance passes, but no major change into how multiplayer works.

What's worse is the dev team has gone silent.  I have said in a number of places that this now seems like a 2019 indie company thinking like a 1995 corporate studio.  I don't know what happened between May and now, but this no longer feels like it's going to get any major updates, and the lack of communication from the dev team on this and other major issues (XBox is *still* unreleased) is frustrating a lot of players.

I still highly recommend the crap out of this game for single player, and the DLC has extended the life of the game for sure.  However, it's a shame that the best multiplayer 6DoF game is going on 24 years old this month, and no game in 20 years has managed to even exceed Descent 3's multiplayer.
[/edit]

[edit2]
Revival Studios is no more, so no more updates will be coming for the game.  They did make a v1.1 update to allow for online play without their own servers, but the experience kind of sucks because there were no changes to the net code.  So, if you really want to play Overload multiplayer, be sure to check out my Steam guide on olmod to learn how to play multiplayer in olmod.  olmod was conceived by Arne de Bruijn, and since has been modified by no less than a dozen other developers who love this game.  It has many improvements and quality of life features that have made multiplayer an awesome experience.
[/edit2]

Honestly, if you ever so much as looked at Descent, this game is worth your while, and at full price, too. Great enemy design, great level design, good weapon variety and the same angry noises coming out of your mouth after a robot sniped you from around a corner on Insane difficulty. 
The only gripe I have with it is the upgrade system, which does feel very forced. Some tier-2 upgrades are pretty nonsensical and only exist to justify having an upgrade system. If you choose the upgrades that *do* make sense, though, there's a neat sense of progression giving you the firepower you need to survive the brutal, brutal endgame levels. Of course you can also play through the game without upgrading anything - there even is an achievement for that - but you'll have a pretty hard time near the end. The actual feature they wanted here was weapon configurability, which can be done through other means; no upgrade system required.

Looking past this, though, the actual gameplay of Overload is exactly what it should be; it's classic Descent action alternating between slow sniper-type battles and frantic enemy ambushes - sometimes in Lockdown-events where you can't escape from the combat area - that force you to make good use of your arsenal or perish. Like the Descents, Overload expects you to play these levels multiple times, gradually learning where each enemy is, where the secret doors that give you upgrade points and ammunition are, and all the while increasing the difficulty level. There's also a NG+ mode with an even more vicious "Insane+" difficulty available - even with the full endgame weapon arsenals and a ton of upgrades, Level 2 on Insane+ already murders your life if you're not careful. The replay value of Overload stems almost entirely from your own skill improving, which is exactly how it should be in a good action game.

Also worth mentioning, the soundtrack is really good; it's made by several composers who did work on the original Descent series and it really gets into your head after a while - the soundtrack from the endgame alien levels in particular is a great experience when you first get there. And I think I even recognized some motifs from Descent 1 somewhere around the Titan Collider level. Honestly, great stuff.

I'd say buy this game, then buy it for all your friends, then even buy it for people you hate. Just give Revival a reason to get back together and make a sequel! ;-)

Absolutely brilliant, recaptures the old Descent nostalgia perfectly and re-packages it for modern tastes. The level design is old-school Descent--minus the claustrophobic tight corridors--and there's not a lot in the way of the more-realistic detail work we're used to seeing in games these days, but I find that I don't really notice the lack. Overload does a really good job striking a balance between the minimalist aesthetics of the old Descent games and the more slick visual fanfare of contemporary titles.

The soundtrack is audiophile heaven. It makes liberal use of the industrial sounds of the Descent 2 soundtrack but is much more symphonic and melodic. Whereas Descent 2's soundtrack was brash and "in your face", Overload's doesn't scream for your attention and just lets you play the game but still has enough cool riffs and beats to stand out. With several different artists in the mix it can sometimes be a mixed bag when styles diverge, but it's still all good. If you're into soundtracks, do yourself a favor and get the package with the soundtrack.

In short, Overload is a must-have for fans of the old series and a great entry to the 6 DOF shooter genre for new fans, and the explosions are pretty enough to keep even the most shameless eye-candy junkie sated. Better yet, it supports VR out of the box and playing with a headset is an absolute blast. Mileage may vary...if you tend to motion sickness you're going to have a bit of a rough go of it. But if you've got the stomach and the chops, VR is the ONLY way to play Overload.

It wouldn't be a good incentive if the upgrade system was lacking, but fortunately its very well done as you upgrade your ship and weapons in between missions. It's no secret that first-person shooters have changed dramatically over the last two decades.  Whereas they once tossed players into labyrinthine levels and expected them to find the exit all by themselves, today they usually take a much more linear, cinematic approach in which exploration is discouraged and the story is force-fed.  Even the recent DOOM reboot, as fantastic as it was, had some awfully straight-forward levels (especially compared to the '93 original) and several unskippable cutscenes.

Well ladies and gentlemen, I'm happy to report that Overload never got the memo.

Made by the creators of Descent, Overload is everything a fan could possibly hope for from a spiritual successor.  It sports prettier graphics and a larger feature set while retaining everything that made the original game so special.  The levels are still as large and complex as ever, weapons and enemies still come in great varieties, and yes, you still have to destroy reactors and run like hell before the whole place explodes.

If you've never before played Descent or any other six-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) shooter, you're in for a trip.  The 6DoF movement system means you can fly in literally every direction and even roll your ship.  Although this can be quite disorienting and even nauseating (especially at first), it also gives you an unprecedented amount of control compared to traditional "grounded" first-person shooters.  It makes combat more exciting, too, since threats can come from any angle and you aren't just limited to strafing left and right in order to avoid incoming fire.

Overload's campaign is broken up into 15 levels, three of which feature boss battles.  Although that might not sound like a large number, the sheer size of these levels means you'll be spending up to half an hour or more on each one.  The levels are so complex, in fact, the developers not only included a full-fledged 3D automap but even implemented a "hologuide" that can be deployed at any time to lead you to the nearest powerup, security key, or even enemy.  Best of all, the levels all play out without any interruptions.  There aren't any cutscenes whatsoever--only collectible audio logs--and even the pre-mission briefings can be skipped in an instant.

Perhaps the biggest change coming from Descent is the addition of an upgrade system which allows you to improve and modify both your ship and weapons over the course of the campaign.  Some examples are the ability to make Missile Pods seek nearby enemies and a big boost to "smash" damage so that you can turn your ship into a powerful battering ram if the need ever arises.  It's worth noting, however, that upgrade points can only be acquired by finding and collecting them, therefore it's strongly encouraged that you explore to your heart's content if you wish to be at your very best going into each new level.

In addition to the campaign, there's also a challenge mode (Overload's take on horde mode) as well as local/online multiplayer.  As someone who's never been a huge fan of multiplayer in these types of games, challenge mode is my personal favorite.  The goal is simple: survive for as long as possible against killer robots that constantly spawn in all around you.  There are 12 arena-like stages to choose from and the more you play, the more XP you earn and the more persistent perks you unlock.  It's admittedly simple, but incredibly fun, highly replayable, and a great way to hone your combat skills.

Perhaps my favorite aspect of Overload aside from its oldschool nature (minimal cutscenes, maximum gameplay) is its vast array of weapons and enemies.  There are 16 different weapons--yes, you can have them all at once--and my favorites include the Crusher, a punishing shotgun that can be upgraded to become fully automatic, and the Devastator, a large missile that explodes into a bomb cluster to deal insane damage.  The enemy variety is even more impressive with over 20 different types of robots.  You'll encounter everything from Guardians, which pester you at long range with precision shots, to sawblade-armed Shredders that launch themselves at you arms-first with very bad intentions.

I also must bring attention to the game's excellent soundtrack.  The audio as a whole is great, from the weapons and explosions to the eerie, mechanical groans emitted by enemies themselves, but the soundtrack is what shines the brightest.  Composed by Dan Wentz, Allister Brimble, and Jerry Berlongieri--all of whom worked on the Descent games--Overload's soundtrack is a perfect revival of the same techno-like musical style that helped make those games so much fun to play and listen to.

Overload is one of those rare titles that, in the process of reviving a long-dead franchise, somehow manages to hit all the right notes.  Even the graphics are surprisingly good, with excellent lighting effects and awesome, over-the-top explosions.  The only complaint I can muster up is that I would've liked to have seen a greater variety of levels and locales, but I'm sure even that will be smoothed out in time thanks to the recently released level editor.  Suffice it to say, if you've been longing for a new Descent or just a new oldschool first-person shooter in general, Overload is like a wish come true and you'd be doing yourself a great disservice to pass it up.

If they ever make a sequel (I hope they do, as unlikely as it is), they need to change the way their level design works. I enjoyed Descent and Descent 2 (never played 3) but the way they do secrets, buttons, and upgrades all feel like they're a major way to drive off players because its such an outdated system. 

Back in the day secret areas block by camouflaged doors was the norm, but now it's just kind of annoying to smash into every hard to notice door trying to figure out if its activated by a button, area trigger, or if it's a monster closet opened by other means. 

Buttons are a pain to figure out because they could activate anything anywhere and are sometimes sealed behind those same secret doors, which may or may not require a button themselves. 

Upgrades points being hidden behind secrets and secrets activated by buttons hidden behind secrets forces the player to constantly scrounge around trying to 100% exploration in the levels which isn't really that fun once again if you have no idea what opens a locked door.

If they make a sequel they could probably find a way to take ques from something like Amid Evil, where secrets were mostly camouflaged by scenery, not sealed off by barely visible doors opened by whatever random means, and buttons were mostly if not always placed where you could directly see what was activated. For buttons far away from the target door, they could have a visual trail like conduits and/or cables.

The upgrade system also felt kinda meh. If it were me I'd have just allowed a secondary effect to each primary weapon. More energy, shields, ammo ect. could have just been pickups like the Doom backpack. Headlights and "sprinting" shouldn't have costed energy anyway.

The game could have also used much brighter lighting. It's nowhere near Doom 3 levels of dark but it is hard to figure out what your looking at most of the time without the headlights.

The enemy designs in Descent felt kinda like fighting 3-4 unique models repurposed with new weapons and armor, Descent 2 felt like it had an actual roster of unique, visually distinct enemies to fight each with their own looks, weapons, movement styles, and strategies. Here, the first 3-4 enemy types looks way too samey and the dark lighting doesn't really help. The only ways I could really tell they were different was the shots from their weapons and how much health they had. At least they kept the Clawbots because those felt like the only enemies I could recognize from a distant, dark hallway.

I keep trying this game but by the time I get to level 5 I'm already burned out from secret hunting (ESPECIALLY secret hunting) and fighting similar enemies in the same very dark corridors. I don't HATE the game, but I can't bring myself to love it. If I can't enjoy it, how could I recommend it to others?

Descent, Descent 2, and Descent 3 were games I was quite into back in the '90s. Such freedom of movement, in regard to not only sliding in various directions, but turning and traveling in various directions as well. It was wild at the time, and as a bit sci-fi fan, I was sold. The music was neat at the time, the gameplay was cool, and there weren't really any other games I played that compared with it. Secrets were fun little temptations to get the next cool weapon one mission before the game practically bounced it off your windshield later on, and it worked. This was essentially the same tactic games like Doom and Doom 2 used in the '90s as well. Great stuff.

Overload is mostly a love letter to Descent in that it feels almost exactly like playing a Descent game with far better graphics, high-quality sound, and even better music than before! The gameplay is slicker/smoother, the new "guide-bot" (or whatever this game calls it) is nice for helping you find enemies, exits, reactors, etc. like in the original, if not better than before, and just...so much is here to love!

However, the way this game handles secrets deviates from the way the original handled them - and by proxy - the way Doom and Doom 2 handled them. Instead, it uses an approach more akin to how Doom 2016 handles secrets. So instead of  just being delayed on obtaining something, you permanently lose it and are gimped the rest of the game. How so? Well, Overload has upgrade spheres hidden around the levels. A few are plain as day, and others are so hidden that I scoured the first mission and only found half of them. There are a limited number of these, and based on the number appearing in each mission, and the number of upgrade points one can spend, if you miss some of these, you will never get all of the upgrades. This is not in line with the premise of the original Descent games, and I find it to be to Overload's detriment.

While I love persistent upgrades, having missable upgrades in a game where you can literally fly in any direction through sprawling maps with hidden doors is counter-intuitive to the exciting pace the original games had. Flying around in Descent 1-3 was exciting and didn't have terrible slow-down. However, if you're having to search everything or get permanently gimped on upgrades, then the pacing is drawn to a screeching halt. Although I overall enjoyed Doom 2016, the '90s Doom games handled pacing far better with their secrets, whereas Doom 2016 had missable persistent upgrades. It was annoying in Doom 2016, but with the additional freedom of movement afforded by Overload, finding all of the persistent upgrades becomes an even more aggravating chore detracting from my enjoyment of the game.

As someone often against games over-relying on nostalgia, I find it surprising to be stating that I would have vastly preferred the original Descent games' approach to secrets and new goodies be used than the Doom 2016 model. I believe that the original way of handling secrets was wholly superior to how Overload handles them.

However, if you just don't care about being permanently gimped as you go through games, or you have fun pausing, looking up a walkthrough for a secret, unpausing, rinse, wash, repeat, until you've found all the upgrades in every mission lest you miss them, then this won't matter to you. =p

[h1]Overall Rating - Seriously Flawed ★★☆☆☆[/h1]

[h1]First Impressions[/h1]
Not since Star Fox 64 back in 1997 have I played many SHMUPs where you don't just look at a small ship from overhead, as piloting a ship in a 3-dimensional manner doesn't seem to arise very often. The only exceptions I'm generally aware of come from jet fighter sims. Regardless, looking at Overload (OL), I was excited for the opportunity to play such a game again. With such positive reviews, I was all too happy to take a key from someone who didn't need it.


[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As already mentioned, this is a first-person perspective SHMUP style game, and true to form you face off against an enemy count that greatly outnumbers you. Your progress carries over from stage to stage, including ammo and energy reserves. At least, I think so, due to the otherwise arbitrary amounts of items you start a stage with, since you don't start off maxed out. Additionally, you're able to upgrade various stats of your ship, such as the power of your weapon systems, speed of the ship, durability, etc. Doing so requires you to find upgrades scattered about each stage, in contrast to gaining XP by killing bad guys. There are also secrets, some of which require careful navigation to find.

Each stage includes progressing objectives. These essentially involve finding keycards to access secured areas, before blowing something of importance to pieces, such as a reactor or boss. Completing the last objective triggers a short count-down before the entire station you're at self-destructs. If you don't escape in time and haven't manually saved during the stage, you would have to start at the very beginning again. You're also able to rescue hibernating people before the base explodes, but more often than not, I can't find where they are and let them die.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2487989336
[h1]Controls[/h1]
Flying a spaceship is surprisingly complicated, but that's because of how much control you have over it. Since you're freely navigating stages in a three dimensional space, you need ways to adjust your trajectory, height, and direction. The controls are fairly intuitive as you get used to them, and give all the tools necessary to fly where you want to go. It takes time to get used to, and it can feel floaty, but the controls work pretty well overall. You also have tools that can be toggled, such as a guide and which weapons system you want to use.


[h1]Story[/h1]
I can't say the story is that interesting, primarily because of how it's delivered. Although it does include voice-overs, you listen to the voice acting while staring at neon green text on a black screen. There aren't cutscenes or images of the people involved to give the events some context, as the only time you'll see the visage of a person is when rescuing people in stasis. Even then it's nothing more than a photo ID. A story is nothing without characters, and the events taking place come across like some paranoid businessman getting ticked off because others won't support his research.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2488112691
[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The locations you fly your ship through exclusively consist of research facilities set in outer space, and excavated tunnels, which doesn't make for the most exciting or diverse environments. For all intents and purposes, it could all be taking place on Earth. In spite of the sterile location, the visuals still look smooth and crisp. Kind of like the environment, enemy ships and the projectiles fired aren't that distinct, but that wasn't what drew my attention to OL in the first place. With my original concerns about the visuals, I'm glad that my orientation in the environment didn't feel obtuse or hard to discern. 


[h1]Sound Design[/h1]
I wouldn't say the music strikes me as spacey, even though the synthetic sounds may have tried to impart that effect, as this is taken over by the consistent style of grungy rock. Some songs slow the tempo down so it's not as aggressive, but I could see all of these songs fitting together on the same CD. It fits the game well enough, though I don't find it to be memorable music either. I didn't mind the voice acting, as infrequent as it might be. Similarly, the sound effects of missiles blowing enemies up, and the other weaponry, sounded as I'd expect from a game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2488112031
[h1]Pros[/h1]
🌟 I didn't notice a lot of difference in the primary weapons, but I could see the distinction more clearly in the secondary ones. This variety helps address different enemy types and situations.
🌟 If you like exploring, there's plenty of secrets hidden in each stage. I doubt you'd find most of them without a guide though.


[h1]Cons[/h1]
❌ The environments aren't broad or open in any sense. You're always flying through tight, compact locations. It somewhat defeats the point of flying a spaceship, because you have no freedom or room to take advantage of your range of flight. 
❌ For whatever reason, I found myself playing the game a mission at a time, not really feeling like playing more of it right away.
❌ Enemies get bullet-spongey quick, so you'll almost have to spend upgrade points on your weapons.


[h1]Tips[/h1]
🔍 With the ammo and other pick-ups available in each stage, you'll want to use your secondary weaponry evenly so that you don't have a slot that still has full ammo and no need for that refill, but are completely empty on something else. Since your weaponry isn't unlimited though, make your shots count.
🔍 Enemies can be tucked away in dead-ends and around blind corners, so you can't be too careful while going into unexplored areas. With how enemies suddenly show up, some won't spawn until you trigger a spawn point.
🔍 Explore the level by yourself for a while before turning on the guide. When I play levels without guidance the whole time, I tend to find more upgrades.


[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
What I enjoyed most while playing OL was the sense of movement as I flew around, and even though some angles might disorient me, it always felt pretty smooth. However, the game itself didn't give me as much satisfaction as I hoped for. The stage design worked against what these controls could have allowed for, putting you into a concise box with almost as little visual interest. With an emphasis on needing to explore for upgrades and secrets, it reminded me of Nintendo 64 games. I remember games from that era hiding power-ups in out of the way locations, and your time in any given stage increased significantly in spite of not accomplishing anything. 

I think the reason why the game gets such good reviews is because it initially feels good. However, the achievements for getting very far into the game aren't earned by many people, with only 15% of people beating the first 3 stages (not including the tutorial). I might recommend OL if I thought more people would even beat it, and since that seems unlikely, I'd suggest skipping it.

Let's start by saying that I've never played a Descent game in my life, so my views are in no way affected by nostalgia.

Six degrees of freedom is, from a design standpoint, both really cool and a very fertile ground for new experiences. But also, because of how uncommon these types of games are, it's a dangerous gamble. The rules are different, the dynamics are different, and the player has to get used to a lot of new concepts, so you can't use the same tools as if you were making a traditional FPS.

I really want to say that Overload nails it. It gets a lot of things right, with really fun combat and visuals, movement feels very nice with a lot of customization options, a compelling, well acted story and loads of content.

But the reality is that it gets more wrong than it gets right. There's a lot to discuss regarding outdated design decisions and problems with the control scheme, but the main issues, for me, reside in the level design.

The navigational issues present in 6DOF games are not helped at all by abstract, Classic Doom-like level design. With such a developed story and lore, you'd think that the levels would be constructed as recognizable bases, science labs, mine shafts, etc. But this is almost never the case. Only late game are some environments used to communicate a place, but still with the same labyrinthine level design, made even worse by the fact that certain very important guiding systems are disabled. In general, nothing identifies what is up, down, left or right, and areas do not flow logically. So, you get lost. A lot. Adding to this the abundance and importance of secrets, most of the game is spent floating around being unsure of where you're going.

There are many other things wrong. The weapon selection system is truly terrible, the default control scheme is weird, and the game kind of overstays its welcome. But most of these thing could be forgiven if the levels were designed with easy navigation in mind. It saddens me, because Revival didn't deserve to go under, and a sequel could have fixed all these issues and made a truly amazing game. And what's here is a fun and unique experience.

I can't sincerely recommend it, unless you're ready for a particular kind of experience. The kind that Descent fans would enjoy. This definitely feels like a game made for the fans, but sometimes, relying on nostalgia ends up working against you.

-CONCLUSION-
The game looks dull all the time, the levels are the same and unmemorable, the story is boring and uninspired, it's so dark so you will be throwing flares everywhere, the weapons are underwhelming (except for 3 i guess), and the sound effects are similar (pew pew). BUT, the AI and core gameplay is remarkable, the music is above average, movement is on point.

Overall, i had very good moments with this game, but i just can't recommend it to anyone because there are so many bad moments i had with being stuck in a dark tunnel, throwing flares everywhere, and interpreting where i was in the automap. COMPASS PLEASE!

This is a game I learned to hate. The single player campaign takes a sharp turn in the last third and  lots of poor game design decisions finally stack up. I didn't finish the game. Bot AI,  flying and dynamic lighting are the best parts of this game. 

[b]Botched control configuration[/b]
Let's start with the stuff that broke the game for me. Later on the game relies on armies of enemies with powerful hit scan weapons. It also forces you to use a weapon you hate. Before that you could use any weapon you like to get stuff done. You *could*  switch to your favorite weapon but bugs and dumb configuration options ruins it.

The selection wheel never matured into a usable tool because you either can't pick a diagonal item or your selection interferes with your movement. You can't assign your favorite weapon(s) either because they are paired. And finally, the slowest fall back method of previous/next selection is broken because it maps internally to “Invert Y”.

Edit: Clarification
This section sounds a bit silly but I fly with joystick and aim with mouse, so buttons are very limited. At this tough stage of the game I'm suddenly and needlessly forced to toggle between two select weapons very fast. Neither the games' options nor my button contingent/configuration allowed that and I never trained it. I could remap everything but at this stage I was already weary, so I decided to quit.

[b]Poor story progression[/b]
Story went from a nice start to lots of short, repetitive chatter to heavy handed crap. 

[b]Environment kills flying[/b]
The environment is heavily stylized with nice textures and a nice color palette. It's rather sterile and lifeless and there are only a few rooms that look truly exciting but I kind of liked it. But I didn't like the overall darkness.

Flying in this game is 50% of the fun. To increase the sense of orientation and movement/speed the environment needs to be visible and close by. Lots of dark areas and (later) black hole textures (the already feeble headlight becomes useless) don't make sense for this game.

[b]Explosions kill motivation[/b]
The explosions also got changed for the worse. 1. No more easily visible flashes indicating a robot death. 2. Heavily darkened debris trails leading to disconnected/confusing debris explosions. 3. Usage of cliche fire textures.

Killing robots became tame, less visually rewarding and less fun. For challenge mode it essentially removed the primary motivation (have fun playing the game) and promoted secondary motivation (play the game to be on the leader boards).

[b]Bright, ear-piercing sounds and annoying music[/b]
I actually tried to play the game without any sound, just to see if I can. It wasn't fun. I settled on -10 db treble, low effects volume and no game music. It's a pity, because I usually liked parts of each track (nice Dark Knight reference) and some sound effects but I couldn't stand the '70s bright whining lead guitars, bright mixes for '80s dull speakers and far too many noise-based, bright, digital, processed, distorted sounds.

Retro games are a curious thing. You can have amazing games with retro graphics and sound and people will love it. But why? What do they have in common? Let's take two recent success stories with Sonia Mania and Shovel Knight.

Sonic Mania - "Exciting level design, a stellar soundtrack, and cool expansions on the original formula"
Sonic Mania - "A breakneck platformer that uses classic Sonic as a foundation for something fresh and exciting. "
Shovel Knight - "Shovel Knight is a modern classic that takes the 2-D platforming genre and modernizes it. "
Shovel Knight - "Old and new in almost the best ways."

What is the common factor here? Both have retro graphics and sound but their gameplay is modern. So what happens when you have a game with modern graphics and retro gameplay? A very mediocre game, thats what. And that is Overload.

When you look at the reviews, you can see that there is a great deal of gushing about how much this is like the old Decent games. The way the ship handles, the enemies, weapons and environments. And they are very, very right. It's like the developers have been locked in hypersleep for the last 20 years and then woke up and decided to make a game. But this isn't what actually happened, they've simply rejected what progress designers have made on how to make games as fun as possible over the years, In their own words, they wanted to bring back what is missing in modern games. Things such as enemies appearing right next to you when you push a button. Remember that from the old days? Opening a doorway with an enemy facing you on the otherside for a free hit. Ahh, that old acorn! Running along face-grinding walls and shooting random surfaces to open hidden stashes of weapons and powerups. Oh, the fun! Enemies that stand perfectly still and silent only to attack without warning as soon as you turn a corner. Every level having the exact same goals with no variety. I won't carry on. Put simply, everything which drags a game down and everything which has been tossed away as refuge by modern games is back! This folks is the Mighty No 9 of 2018 - the wrong kind of retro.

The level design and balance is equally as poor, with you frequently being fired upon down narrow corridors where you have no room to dodge and you need to back up to the nearest corner to play peek-a-boo. Whole rooms cleared because you went in, backed out and then just shot the bots as they came through the narrow doorway one by one making the whole affair a tedious chore. Enemies dropping health like candy because the developers haven't got the hang of enemy placement and map layout so in order to keep you alive they have to keep throwing health at you. Powerups, like invulnerability, hidden in secret compartments well away from the action so when you do get them they're utterly useless. There is also the questionable fact that it is impossible for them to carefully design levels to be fair for the player when their difficulty system increases the projectile speed of enemies. So if you're in a room with a bot at the other end and you can just narrowly avoid incoming fire on the lowest setting, it then becomes impossible on the high settings. Same room, same bot placement but with a completely different result. Suddenly you need cover but none is provided.

But it's not all doom and gloom. The music is nice and the graphics are decent. But Overload is simply the wrong way to do retro games. It tugs on the nostalgia by including hi-scores and Decent-like gameplay but it ends up being mediocre because it revived all of the great things about the series along with all the bad game design habits that should stay in the past. Not recommended at all.

As someone who still plays classic Descent to this day, I really wanted to love this game. Don't get me wrong, it's still pretty fun and you should give it a go if you're curious. However, it definitely falls short in a few places. Mainly in the weapons and enemy design, and probably my biggest complaint is how poorly optimized it is. My computer is no powerhouse but it should not have trouble running something like this, and massive framerate drops happen consistently. Also aiming feels sluggish. I think they were trying to make it feel more like piloting a space ship but for FPS controls to feel so imprecise is a big issue.

Pros:
-good level design
-the graphics do look good when they aren't throttling your machine
-upgrade system adds interesting depth but is pretty basic
-robot spawners are a huge improvement
-secrets are complex and actually recorded in the stats
-classic Descent style gameplay 
-some new weapons are cool
-many well made community levels
-many survival challenges if you enjoy that
-music

The biggest changes from the classic formula are the upgrade system, life system, and survival challenges. Also kind of a tangent, but robot makers in Descent are by far the most tedious part of the game. Basically forcing you to sit in one spot slowly killing robots or get shot in the back. By making spawners destructible, it creates a high priority target while forcing you juggle surrounding enemies. Creates some exciting fights that require a lot of maneuvering. 

Having a life system may be divisive, but it's one of my favorite parts of the original. Never having to worry about saving or restarting a whole fight keep things moving in a big way. Taking a death is worth it if you can destroy a big chunk out of enemies and if you make a mistake it doesn't ruin your run. It also gives incentive to play higher difficulties by providing higher score/more lives for the extra challenge. In addition, it makes rescuing hostages an important decision. The risk of collecting them early and dying adds a lot of tension. Rescuing civilians here feels like some weird hold over since if you die you'll need to load a save anyway. May as well not even be there.

Survival challenges have been made a major focus here, completely replacing secret levels. You must destroy a certain number of enemies for an upgrade point. This can actually really hurt you if you enter the challenge too injured, or when you return having used all your resources. There are a ton of challenges to be found from the main menu but must be unlocked through an arbitrary system and are completely separate from the main game. If you like arcade style survival and high score chasing, then this is a major feature! Online leader boards let you compete with others. It doesn't really appeal to me though, and feels like that took focus away from the main game.

Cons:
-very little enemy variety / look almost identical / weapon variants make identifying pointless anyway
-secret hunting is required for upgrade points
-many weapons aren't available until the very end
-many weapons are redundant
-short campaign with generic af plot
-aiming sucks??
-too much focus on survival challenges
-runs very poorly on mid range machines
-no upgrading for the last quarter leaving you with many unused points
-basically no environment variety, play a few levels and you've seen them all
